evidence_text:
High-sensitivity pan-cancer AI assessment of lymph node metastasis via uncertainty quantification. The histological heterogeneity of primary tumors across the pan-cancer spectrum poses a formidable barrier to accurate lymph node metastasis assessment, often causing AI systems to make "overconfident errors" on rare variants that lead to missed diagnoses. To address this, we present UPATHLN, a unified diagnostic platform that synergizes a pathology foundation model-based encoder with a decoupled uncertainty estimation mechanism. We developed and validated the system using a large-scale multicentre dataset of 26,229 lymph nodes from 14 distinct primary origins. In internal validation, UPATHLN achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.986. Crucially, the uncertainty module functioned as a decisive fail-safe: by flagging potential false-negative predictions for mandatory pathologist review, it intercepted all missed diagnoses, securing 100% conditional sensitivity across both the development and independent test cohorts-even for tumors from seven unseen primary origins. Concurrently, this mechanism reduced the review burden on negative lymph nodes by 73.2%. Ultimately, UPATHLN sets a new benchmark for safety-critical AI, demonstrating that explicitly modeling uncertainty is key to unlocking reliable, workload-efficient diagnostics at the pan-cancer scale. Introduction  Cancer remains a leading cause of death worldwide  1  , primarily driven by metastasis  2 , 3  . Lymph nodes (LNs) are critical anatomical checkpoints in cancer progression  4  , serving as initial metastatic sites and immune regulatory hubs orchestrating host-tumor interactions  5  . Accurate assessment of lymph node metastasis (LNM) status is therefore paramount for prognostic assessment and therapeutic decision-making across diverse cancer types  6  . However, current clinical management relies primarily on crude quantitative approaches—predominantly pN staging  6  —which fail to capture crucial biological features such as lymph node ratio (LNR), metastatic tumor burden, and diverse spatial growth patterns of metastatic cells within LNs. Recent evidence explicitly links elevated LNR to decreased survival rates and shortened recurrence-free intervals  7  , while highlighting how spatial distributions of metastatic cells can modulate the immune microenvironment, potentially facilitating immune escape  8  . Despite these insights, pathologists now face an unprecedented surge in LN specimens due to rising cancer incidence  9  , rendering such detailed, multi-dimensional analysis practically unfeasible in routine workflows.  Deep learning has rapidly advanced pathological diagnosis, with numerous artificial intelligence (AI) systems gaining regulatory approval. However, existing AI approaches for LNM detection  10 – 15   typically follow cancer-specific paradigms. This fragmentation hinders widespread clinical adoption by necessitating multiple, disparate systems  16 , 17  , conflicting with the need for operational efficiency and unified diagnostic standards. Moreover, tumor heterogeneity manifests as a “long-tail distribution”  18 , 19  , where common metastatic patterns coexist with diverse rare variants. Standard deep learning models often struggle with these outliers, prone to “overconfident errors” where the system makes incorrect predictions with high certainty on out-of-distribution data. The reliable detection of these rare but clinically significant variants is crucial for patient safety  20 , 21  , yet remains challenging even with large datasets. While emerging foundation models  22 – 27   offer powerful representational capabilities, their effective application across the pan-cancer spectrum requires substantial annotation resources. Thus, there is an urgent need to transcend these limitations and establish a unified, robust, and safe diagnostic framework capable of not only high sensitivity but also reliable failure awareness across all cancer types.  To address these challenges, we developed UPATHLN, a unified, uncertainty-aware AI platform integrating a pathology foundation model with uncertainty-guided active learning and robust uncertainty estimation (Fig.  1 ). Trained and validated on an extensive multi-center, multi-cancer LN dataset, this study demonstrates UPATHLN’s capacity for highly sensitive and safe pan-cancer LNM detection with robust generalization. Ultimately, this study represents a critical step towards establishing a unified, trustworthy diagnostic standard for AI-assisted pathology.    Fig. 1   Development of clinically safe pan-cancer lymph node pathology diagnostic system.   a  Multi-center data composition: clinical samples from three hospitals of varying scales covering lymph nodes (LNs) from 14 primary sites.  b  Surgical case complexity: each case typically involves >10 LNs, increasing diagnostic workload compared to primary tumor assessment.  c  Representative HE examples of lymph node metastases illustrating morphological heterogeneity. Insets highlight thyroid-type colloid-like material and other non-specific patterns that may be prominent in metastases from the indicated primary sites, including mucin pools, stromal fibrosis/desmoplasia, and keratin pearls.  d  Uncertainty-guided active learning framework: system leverages clinical pathology database with iterative refinement where pathologists review high uncertainty (HU) predictions, verify challenging cases through IHC staining (CAM5.2, AE1/3), and exclude poor-quality samples. In clinical practice, uncertainty estimates guide pathologists' review to prevent rare subtype misdiagnosis and enable continuous system improvement.                     Results   Establishment of the UPATHLN platform and active learning optimization  To establish the UPATHLN platform, we curated a large-scale, multi-center pan-cancer dataset comprising 26,229 lymph nodes (LNs) from 8294 whole-slide images (WSIs) across 2738 patients, spanning tumors from 14 distinct primary organs. The dataset was rigorously partitioned into a development cohort and an independent test cohort, with seven rare primary origins strictly held out as unseen primary-origin holdouts to evaluate generalization to previously unseen origins (SFig.  1 ). To ensure high-quality input to the platform, our automated LN extraction pipeline achieved robust performance, with YOLOv8-s demonstrating a recall of 0.994 (95% CI: 0.990–0.998) for LN detection and nnUNet achieving a Dice score of 0.934 (95% CI: 0.923–0.945) for tissue segmentation, effectively excluding non-target tissues (Fig.  2a  and SFig.  2 ).    Fig. 2   Deep learning framework for lymph node metastasis detection with iterative refinement.   a  System architecture overview. The pipeline sequentially employs a detection model to localize lymph node regions and a segmentation model to delineate their contours. The core classification framework features a Multiscale Cross-Attention architecture that utilizes the UNI pathology foundation model as a feature encoder. By synthesizing features from multi-scale tissue patches, the model simultaneously outputs tumor confidence via the Classification Module and prediction uncertainty via the Uncertainty Estimation Module.  b – e  Performance metrics comparing original and high uncertainty (HU)-filtered predictions across training iterations: tile-level AUC ( b ), PPV ( c ), NPV ( d ), and lymph node-level sensitivity ( e ).  f ,  g  Lymph node-level metrics: average false positives (FPavg) and average high uncertainty regions (HUavg). At the lymph-node level, each LN was counted once regardless of the number of false-positive or high-uncertainty subregions within it. In bar charts ( b – g ), 95% confidence intervals were derived from bootstrapping (1000 iterations).                   Rather than relying on static training, we optimized the platform using an uncertainty-driven active learning strategy. Misclassified tiles were enriched in the high-uncertainty (HU) tail of the tile-level uncertainty-score distribution (SFig.  4a ). Accordingly, we summarized tile uncertainties into a slide-level ambiguity score and ranked candidate WSIs for expert review (SFig.  3 , “Methods”). Through five rounds of human-in-the-loop iterations, this active optimization substantially improved discriminative performance on the internal validation set, increasing the tile-level AUC from a baseline of 0.953 (95% CI: 0.932–0.974) to 0.986 (95% CI: 0.976–0.996), with consistent gains in both PPV and NPV (Fig.  2b–d ).  To rigorously attribute this high performance to architectural design rather than data accumulation alone, we benchmarked the final model against alternative architectures trained on the identical dataset generated from the final iteration. The multiscale architecture significantly outperformed both the single-scale UNI baseline (AUC = 0.928, 95% CI: 0.910–0.946; DeLong test,  P  < 0.0001) and the ImageNet-pretrained feature extractor (AUC = 0.918, 95% CI: 0.901–0.935; DeLong test,  P  < 0.0001; SFig.  4b ).    Uncertainty-aware classification achieves high-sensitivity LNM detection  Crucially, the parallel uncertainty estimation module functioned as a clinical fail-safe. While the optimized multiscale classifier achieved a robust intrinsic sensitivity of 0.996 (95% CI: 0.985–1.000; Fig.  2e ), it erroneously classified three metastatic cases as negative when relying exclusively on diagnostic probability scores (false negatives, FNs). In the uncertainty-annotated confusion matrix (SFig.  5a ; HU-flag counts are shown in parentheses), all three FNs were flagged as high uncertainty and therefore routed for mandatory pathologist confirmation. This capability to “rescue” potential false negatives effectively neutralized the risk of missed diagnosis, underpinning the system’s 100% conditional sensitivity and ensuring that ambiguous but critical lesions were correctly routed for pathologist confirmation.  To evaluate clinical workload, we quantified the review burden at the LN level. Here, each LN was counted at most once, regardless of how many false-positive or high-uncertainty subregions it contained. Across iterations, both the LN-level false-positive (FP) rate and HU rate steadily declined (Fig.  2f, g ), reaching final values of 0.112 (95% CI: 0.070–0.155) and 0.156 (95% CI: 0.110–0.202), respectively. The model’s progressive refinement was visually corroborated by prediction heatmaps (Fig.  3a  and SFig.  6 ), and it precisely identified diverse metastatic burdens, including macro-metastases, micro-metastases, and isolated tumor cell clusters (Fig.  3b ). Final validation by pathologists on the remaining development cohort confirmed a 100% positive detection rate with minimal review overhead (1% FP rate and 0.16% HU rate at the LN level).    Fig. 3   Visualization of iterative refinement and representative challenging cases.   a  Representative lymph node whole-slide images (WSIs) with prediction heatmaps from the first iteration and the final (fifth) iteration, showing progressive refinement across active-learning cycles. Right, a magnified example tile from the high-uncertainty (HU) regions identified in the first iteration.  b  Representative isolated LNM detection cases with immunohistochemical (IHC) validation. For each case, the HE slide, the registered IHC section, and the corresponding prediction heatmap are shown, with magnified tumor tiles from the boxed regions. In the magnified panels, orange arrowheads on HE indicate tumor cell foci, and the corresponding IHC images highlight tumor cells by brown chromogenic staining. In the heatmaps, yellow denotes HU regions, red denotes regions with high tumor confidence, and blue denotes lymph node tissue. Scale bars as indicated.                     Validation of pan-cancer robustness and safety  Performance evaluation on the independent test cohort confirmed the system’s robust discriminative power (Fig.  4  and SFig.  7 – 10 ). To establish a baseline, we first evaluated the standalone classification module without uncertainty intervention. Operating strictly on diagnostic probability scores, the module achieved a robust sensitivity of 98.7% and a specificity of 88.0% (SFig.  5b ). Although this represents a high level of diagnostic accuracy, relying solely on this conventional probability thresholding still resulted in 60 FN predictions (missed LNMs). Crucially, the parallel uncertainty estimation module functioned as a decisive fail-safe mechanism to address this residual risk. It successfully intercepted all 60 initially missed instances by classifying them as HU. This “rescue effect” secured a 100% conditional sensitivity across the entire test cohort, effectively neutralizing the clinical risk of missed diagnoses.    Fig. 4   Pan-cancer generalization performance across 14 primary origins.  The multi-center multi-cancer independent test cohort is stratified into common and rare origins. Primary sites are sorted by WSI count and color-coded: purple (Trained) and mint green (Unseen). Rows display: (1) Total WSI counts; (2) Metastatic status distribution (red: metastatic; blue: non-metastatic); (3) LN-level conditional sensitivity (maintaining 100% via uncertainty referral); (4) False Positive (FP) rate; and (5) High Uncertainty (HU) rate. Color intensity reflects numerical magnitude.                   The operational cost of this safety profile was quantified using the Review Burden Rate on Negative Cases (RBR-N). Accounting for the union of FP and HU predictions, the effective RBR-N was 26.8% (3180/11,873). This indicates that 73.2% of negative LNs were safely excluded from manual review.  Subgroup analysis revealed remarkable consistency across organ origins, with a weighted average FP rate of 7.5% (SD: 2.1%) (Fig.  4 ). For the seven cancer types included in training, performance remained stable regardless of sample size. Notably, although Stomach cancer LNs were overrepresented in the training data (35.6%), their performance (HU rate: 5.2%; FP rate: 6.6%) closely mirrored the cohort average, indicating that the model maintained balanced discriminative power despite the non-uniform training distribution. While robust to sample size variations, the model exhibited sensitivity to specific non-neoplastic histological features. LNs from the lung and cervix exhibited higher HU rates (32.6% and 26.0%, respectively). Pathological audit confirmed that in lung cancer, these flags were predominantly triggered by anthracitic pigment, indicating that the model correctly identified non-malignant confounders as HU regions (SFig.  11 ).  Most notably, the system demonstrated exceptional adaptability to the seven cancer types entirely unseen during training. The fail-safe mechanism remained fully effective even in these out-of-distribution domains, with zero missed diagnoses recorded. Regarding efficiency, the model maintained consistently low LN-level FP rates for the majority of these unseen origins (6/7), ranging from 2.4% (kidney) to 10.8% (thyroid) without fine-tuning. The sole exception was penile cancer (SFig.  8 ), a rare type with complex morphology, where the system exhibited an adaptive increase in review rates (HU: 30.2%; FP: 20.0%). This reflects a cautious inference strategy that prioritizes diagnostic safety when encountering highly atypical histological patterns.    Interpretability and pathological characterization of uncertainty  To elucidate the interpretability underlying this robust performance, we deconstructed the uncertainty landscape. Multiscale feature fusion dimensionality reduction analysis (Fig.  5a, b ) clearly delineated tumor and normal regions, with HU areas concentrated at the boundaries in feature space. We were able to effectively extract these areas through uncertainty quantification.    Fig. 5   Visualization and interpretation of uncertainty estimation.   a ,  b  t-SNE visualization of tile-level feature embeddings from the internal validation dataset.  a  Binary prediction distribution (red: tumor; blue: normal), with triangles indicating misclassified samples.  b  Uncertainty level distribution (yellow: High Uncertainty [HU]; blue: Low Uncertainty [LU]), showing HU samples concentrating at the tumor-normal decision boundary.  c  Pathological categorization of HU clusters identifying four non-neoplastic confounders: dense connective tissue (orange), loose connective tissue (teal), bleeding (green), and low-quality regions (blue).  d  Representative heatmaps displaying spatial distributions of HU regions (yellow) alongside tumor (red) and normal (blue) predictions.  e  Clinical workflow illustration: HU predictions trigger pathologist re-review, with IHC confirmation reserved for challenging cases.                   Further analysis allowed categorization of HU regions into types such as dense connective tissue, loose connective tissue, low-quality image areas, and bleeding areas (Fig.  5c ). As shown in Fig.  5d , the model assigned high HU scores to two patients with distinct atypical cytomorphology: one with lymphocyte-like tumor cells featuring scant cytoplasm and naked nuclei, and another exhibiting plasmacytoid/histiocytoid features with moderate cytoplasm. This assessment mechanism enables pathologists to selectively focus on these challenging cases, thereby ensuring diagnostic accuracy and clinical safety while improving efficiency. As the system continues to be applied, manual review of uncertain regions will facilitate ongoing model optimization (Fig.  5e ).     Discussion  This study addresses the limitations of current organ-specific AI paradigms by presenting UPATHLN, a unified, uncertainty-aware framework for pan-cancer LNM diagnosis. While previous deep learning approaches have validated LNM detection in organ-specific cohorts, they often operate as “black boxes,” lacking the safety mechanisms required for broad clinical adoption  20  . By devising a specialized Multiscale cross-attention framework to effectively contextualize features from the pathology foundation model, UPATHLN establishes a robust clinical safety net. Notably, this architectural design demonstrated a definitive “fail-safe” capability in a large-scale independent cohort: the uncertainty mechanism successfully intercepted all initially missed metastases, securing 100% conditional sensitivity. This achievement marks a significant advancement: moving from algorithms that prioritize raw accuracy to safety-critical systems that effectively mitigate the risk of FNs in metastatic screening.  The parallel uncertainty estimation branch underpins the technical integrity of this safety profile. Classical uncertainty estimation methods—such as uncertainty-prediction model co-training  28 , 29  , multiple model ensembles  30  , or repeated dropout strategies  28 , 31  —increase computational burden and often flag large unnecessary regions for manual reassessment. By contrast, our independent bypass architecture provides precise localization of diagnostically uncertain regions without compromising inference speed. This decoupled mechanism acts as a reliable diagnostic filter, specifically designed to handle the inherent biological heterogeneity of metastatic disease. It respects the ambiguity of “long-tail” rare variants and non-neoplastic confounders (e.g., anthracotic pigment), routing these cases strictly within the system’s competence boundaries. This “rescue effect” ensures that algorithmic limitations do not translate into diagnostic errors, maintaining high reliability even when encountering complex morphologies that typically confound conventional models.  Furthermore, we successfully navigated the data annotation bottleneck that typically constrains the scalability of foundation models. By coupling high-level feature representations with an uncertainty-guided active learning framework, we efficiently captured a comprehensive spectrum of metastatic morphologies across 14 cancer types without necessitating exhaustive annotation. This strategy proved vital for addressing the diverse patterns of metastatic pathology. Consequently, the system maintained robust performance even on LNM samples from primary sites entirely unseen during training. This demonstrates that uncertainty-driven learning provides a practical, scalable pathway to generalize pathology AI, enabling adaptability to domain shifts and rare cancer types lacking large-scale training data.  UPATHLN reconciles the critical tension between rising diagnostic volumes and the demand for granular prognostic assessment. By safely automating the exclusion of 73.2% of negative LNs, the system liberates pathologists to focus on complex cases. Crucially, this efficiency renders detailed “multi-dimensional analysis”—specifically the precise quantification of tumor-to-lymph node area ratio  12   and spatial distribution patterns—feasible in routine practice. Moving beyond crude pN staging, UPATHLN provides the quantitative depth required for modern precision oncology that is practically impossible to achieve manually.  Despite these advances, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, this study is retrospective, and all training/validation data were sourced from hospitals in China; therefore, real-world deployment requires prospective multi-center evaluation and external validation across diverse populations, institutions, and scanning protocols. Second, although many artifacts are appropriately flagged as high uncertainty, future work could incorporate dedicated artifact-suppression or quality-control modules to further reduce review burden without compromising safety. Third, while the pipeline is designed to be compatible with different pathology foundation models, we only evaluated UNI and did not empirically compare performance against alternative encoders.  Collectively, UPATHLN advances pan-cancer LNM screening by introducing a risk-aware architecture that balances automation with expert oversight. The synergy between its decoupled uncertainty “fail-safe” and active learning framework ensures robust performance and scalability under heterogeneous clinical conditions. This approach not only streamlines routine triage but also provides a quantitative basis for assessing metastatic burden, potentially informing prognostic insights beyond standard pathological staging.    Methods   Dataset collection and cohort definition  We established a large-scale, pan-cancer dataset combining clinical data from three independent medical centers, with heterogeneous clinical workloads and patient populations, enabling evaluation across varied real-world settings. The primary clinical cohort included 2738 patients (8294 WSIs, 26,229 LNs) covering 14 distinct solid tumor types (SFig.  1a ). We applied specific exclusion criteria to ensure data quality: WSIs exhibiting severe artefacts—such as tissue folding covering >20% of the area, significant out-of-focus blurring, or extreme staining inconsistencies—were removed prior to analysis. In addition to the clinical cohort, we utilized an annotated gastric cancer dataset from our previous work  12   (GLN21) and the publicly available breast cancer dataset from the CAMELYON16 challenge  11   (BLN16) for model initialization.  Crucially, to prevent data leakage, we employed a strict patient-level splitting strategy, where all WSIs and LN sections from the same patient were assigned exclusively to a single cohort. As illustrated in the study design flow (SFig.  3 ), the clinical data were stratified into two independent cohorts. The development cohort consisted of 683 patients (2547 WSIs, 9729 LNs) from 7 common cancer types and was further subdivided to support the active learning workflow (SFig.  1b ). The multi-center multi-cancer test cohort comprised an independent set of 2055 patients (5747 WSIs, 16,500 LNs), serving as the held-out standard for final performance evaluation (SFig.  1c ). To rigorously assess the model’s generalization capabilities, the test cohort was stratified into two groups: the 7 cancer types encountered during training and a distinct set of 7 cancer types (thyroid, pancreas, bile duct, kidney, prostate, penis, and anus). Crucially, samples from these rare origins were strictly excluded from the training pipeline, ensuring that their evaluation represents a true test of the model’s ability to generalize to completely unseen primary origins. For LN counting, pathologists manually reviewed the slides to identify spatially distinct LNs; serial sections of the same node, if present, were identified based on morphological continuity and excluded from the total count to ensure each observation represented a unique LN.  This retrospective, multi-center study was conducted in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations and the Declaration of Helsinki. The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Changhai Hospital (CHEC2024-276), the Ethics Committee of the Second People’s Hospital of Wuxi (2024Y-125), and the Ethics Committee of the 960th Hospital of the People’s Liberation Army (2024-087). The requirement for informed consent was waived because of the retrospective design and the use of anonymized data.    Lymph node contour recognition  To increase the training accuracy of LN metastasis detection models, we first developed an LN contour recognition model. The WSIs of LN tissue include not only LNs but also muscle, extraneous fat, and cancer nodules. The presence of these nontarget tissues can adversely affect the accuracy of metastasis detection.  Our model comprises two stages: initially, the YOLOv8-s model is employed for LN detection due to its high efficiency and rapid localization capabilities. The detected regions are subsequently input into the nnUNet  32   model for segmentation to remove impurities from the LN periphery.  We processed images using 1024 × 1024 pixel tiles at 1× magnification and utilized a 256-pixel sliding window for segmentation. The YOLOv8-s model was trained with default parameters, using the annotated contour coordinates as ground truth labels. The nnUNet model was similarly trained with default settings, using the bounding box of annotated regions to cut tiles at 0.25× magnification and employing annotated contours as masks.  During inference, a staged strategy was employed: YOLOv8-s model-predicted coordinates were used to cut local tiles, which were then input into the nnUNet model to obtain precise contour masks. These masks were mapped back to the full 0.25x thumbnail based on relative coordinates. For overlapping sliding windows, an averaging method was used to smooth boundaries.  We annotated 200 WSIs with 721 LNs from various tumor types for the YOLOv8-s model and nnUNet model training. After initial training, predictions of unannotated WSIs in the development cohort were manually reviewed. We reviewed 918 WSIs (comprising 3528 LNs) and reannotated 132 WSIs with incorrect predictions. Then, the YOLOv8-s model was retrained on a combined dataset of the initial 200 annotated WSIs and the 918 manually reviewed WSIs (total 1118 WSIs; randomly split into 80% training and 20% testing). Ultimately, the YOLOv8-s model achieved a recall rate of 0.994 (95% CI: 0.990–0.998) for LN detection.  Since nnUNet requires contour-level annotations, we used the initial 200 WSIs along with the 132 fully corrected WSIs (comprising 1245 LNs) for retraining. Finally, the nnUNet model achieved a mean Dice score of 0.934 (95% CI: 0.923–0.945) for LN contour segmentation. A manual review of inference results from the development cohort confirmed the ability of the two-stage model to accurately delineate LN contours and exclude non-LN tissues. This process provides high-quality input data for subsequent metastasis detection. As illustrated in SFig.  2a , we effectively identified and extracted LN contours from complex pathological images, facilitating high-quality input for further metastasis detection. Some missed LN diagnoses are due to atypical morphology (e.g., indistinct capsules) or small nodal size (SFig.  2b ). In clinical applications, missed LN identification is rare, so it does not increase the workload. Pathologists can easily add annotations during the review process. As missed diagnosis cases continue to be collected, this situation will become increasingly rare. The annotation and review process was conducted by two senior pathologists with over 15 years of experience: Y.C. and C.Q.    Data preprocessing for the classification model  Following the extraction of LN contour regions from WSIs, we tiled tumor metastasis areas on the basis of annotations to train the classification model. Given that accurate diagnosis of some LN metastases requires multiscale observations, we applied multiscale tiling to the annotated dataset. This process involved extracting image tiles of size 256 × 256 pixels at both 10x and 4× magnification, as shown in Fig.  2a . The center coordinates of tiles at both scales were aligned to ensure consistent observation of the same region at different resolutions.  By integrating the LN contour mask with the tumor mask, we cropped regions of interest into tumor and nontumor areas. At 10× magnification, a sliding window of 64 pixels was used to divide the region into extractable tiles, with each grid classified on the basis of the proportion of the tumor area annotated by doctors. Specifically, if more than 25% of a grid area was annotated as a tumor, the tile was labeled positive; otherwise, it was labeled negative. To ensure category balance, if the number of tiles in any category exceeded 100 within a WSI, we randomly selected 100 tiles. This sampling strategy maintained balanced categories at the tile level.    Feature extractor  In this study, we utilized UNI  23  , a Vision Transformer (ViT-Large  33  ) foundation model pre-trained on over 100,000 HE-stained WSIs, as a frozen feature extractor. UNI was selected as it represented a leading solution for pan-cancer feature representation at the time of study implementation. Importantly, our proposed multiscale architecture is designed to be foundation-model agnostic. While UNI was employed here as a representative high-performance encoder to validate our framework, the system is compatible with and can readily incorporate other emerging pathology foundation models  22 , 24 – 27  . For feature extraction, we processed image tiles of size 256 × 256 pixels at both the 10× and the 4× magnification levels and randomly cropped them to 224 × 224 pixels. The resulting feature matrix for each tile maintains a shape of (196 + 1, 1024), where 196 represents the length of the patch-tokens, and 1 represents the class token.    Multiscale feature fusion and classification module  By extracting features from the same local region at different magnification levels and then fusing them, the model can capture both global and local pathological morphological features, better locating and identifying tumor areas. Specifically, we adopted the cross-attention module proposed by Zhou et al.  34   to multiscale image feature fusion. As shown in Fig.  2a , the entire cross-attention module consists of two cross-attention blocks and two self-attention blocks. The cross-attention blocks learn the intrinsic connections of multiscale image features by dynamically weighting features from different spatial scales.  In the cross-attention block, the process of generating Q, K, and V for each scale image feature is as follows:   1      Q    4  x    ,    K    4  x    ,    V    4  x    =  LP     Norm       X    4  x              2      Q    10  x    ,    K    10  x    ,    V    10  x    =  LP     Norm       X    10  x             where     LP     ⋅        denotes linear projection and     Norm     ⋅        denotes layer normalization. The forwards pass in the cross-attention block can be summarized as:   3      P    4  x    =  Attn  (    Q    4  x  ′      K    4  x  ,      V    4  x    )  +  Attn  (    Q    4  x    ,    K    10  x    ,    V    10  x    )      4      P    10  x    =  Attn  (    Q    10  x    ,    K    10  x    ,    V    10  x    )  +  Attn  (    Q    10  x    ,    K    4  x    ,    V    4  x    )     where     Attn  (    Q    4  x    ,    K    4  x    ,    V    4  x      ) and     Attn  (    Q    10  x    ,    K    10  x    ,    V    10  x    )     capture the intra-scale feature relationships. The intermediate expression  P  represents the potential connections obtained through interaction between the 4x and 10× magnification images. The attention mechanism     Attn     Q  ,  K  ,  V        includes two matrices multiplication operations, a scaling operation, and a softmax operation:   5    Attn  (  Q  ,  K  ,  V  )  =  softmax         QK    T          d    k           V     where    T    denotes the matrix transpose operator and     d  k     is the scaling hyperparameter set to 64. Next, the residual learning approach incorporates the resulting  P   4x   and  P   10x   into the normalization layer and multiple layer perceptron (MLP):   6      X    4  x    ′  =  MLP  (  Norm  (    P    4  x    )  )  +    X    4  x        7      X    10  x    ′  =  MLP     Norm     P  10  x        +    X    10  x       where     X   4    x   ′       and     X   10    x   ′       represent the inputs fed into the next cross-attention block.  Subsequently, we merged the cross-attention features by concatenating the tokens directly, resulting in a new feature embedding with a shape of (197 + 197,1024).  Finally, we input the new feature embedding into two self-attention modules, followed by LayerNorm normalization. The class token from the feature embedding is then used as the overall feature  F , which is fed into a fully connected layer to predict the tumor probability of the 10x tile.  During training, the parameters of the UNI pretrained ViT-Large feature extractor were fixed, and no backpropagation optimization was performed. We used ColorJitter from Torchvision for transformation with the following parameters: maximum increments of 0.1 for brightness, 0.2 for contrast, 0.2 for saturation, and 0.15 for hue. The tiles were also randomly flipped and rotated by 15°. To address the imbalance between positive and negative samples, we perform balanced sampling of positive and negative samples at the initialization of each epoch. We calculated the loss via cross-entropy between the predicted probabilities and the true labels and optimized it via adaptive moment estimation with weight decay (AdamW) during training, with a weight decay of 0.05 and a batch size of 64. The learning rate was managed via a cosine annealing schedule, starting at 1e-4, peaking at 5e-4 and ending at 1e-6 over 40 epochs. All training and testing were performed on six NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs.    Uncertainty estimation module  Deploying deep learning models across multi-center pan-cancer cohorts inevitably introduces challenges related to histological heterogeneity, variable data quality, and out-of-distribution inputs that essentially differ from the training distribution. In such scenarios, enforcing deterministic predictions often leads to high-confidence errors. To address this, we incorporated a parallel uncertainty estimation module into our diagnostic framework. The primary objective of this module is to quantify the reliability of region-level predictions, serving a dual purpose: guiding model optimization through active learning during development and acting as a trigger for pathologist review during clinical inference.  Diverging from conventional approaches that rely on computationally expensive ensembles or require joint training with classification objectives (which may destabilize the primary task)  28 – 31  , we implemented a sequential optimization strategy. Specifically, the uncertainty branch is trained as an independent architectural bypass only after the multiscale classifier parameters are frozen. This design ensures that the uncertainty mechanism is specifically calibrated to the fixed decision boundary of the main model. Consequently, this approach enables precise confidence estimation without compromising the original diagnostic performance, while incurring negligible computational overhead.  Specifically, we implemented this module by adapting the uncertainty estimation algorithm for pretrained models proposed by Kirchhof et al .   35  . As shown in Fig.  2a , using the same feature  F  as the classification model input, we passed it through the uncertainty estimation module comprising three fully connected layers with 512 hidden units and LeakyReLU intermediate activations, outputting a single value normalized by the Softplus function to ensure positivity. We used mean squared error (MSE) loss, comparing the uncertainty module’s predictions with labels derived from the classification model’s forward propagation loss, computed at runtime with backpropagation disabled. Crucially, this design provides an intuitive measure of reliability: a high predicted loss indicates that the model anticipates a likely error on the input, thereby flagging it as a “High Uncertainty” (HU) region for pathologist review.  The loss function is defined as:   8     L  uncertainty   =   1  N    ∑   i  =  1   N        u  i   −   L   pred  i       2      where    u    is the uncertainty module’s predicted value and      L    pred      is the loss from the classification model’s forwards propagation.  The training process employed the same data and sampling strategy as those of the classification module. We used the AdamW optimizer with a weight decay of 0.05 and a batch size of 64. The learning rate followed a cosine annealing schedule, starting at 1e-4, peaking at 5e-4 and decreasing to 1e-6 over 10 epochs.    Uncertainty-driven active learning strategy  To address tumor heterogeneity and optimize annotation efficiency, we implemented a human-in-the-loop, uncertainty-driven active learning framework structured into five distinct iterations (Fig.  1d  and SFig.  3 ). To facilitate this process, the clinically derived development cohort (683 patients) was partitioned into two functional subsets via random patient-level sampling: a large unlabeled candidate pool of 594 patients (2245 WSIs, 8832 LNs) available for selection, and a strictly held-out internal validation set of 89 patients (302 WSIs, 897 LNs). Notably, the internal validation set was comprehensively annotated at the lesion level prior to the active learning process. This set remained fixed throughout the study and served as a reliable ground truth to monitor model convergence and determine hyperparameters without biasing the training process.  The training workflow commenced with an initialization phase (Iteration 1), where the baseline model was trained solely on the fully annotated initialization datasets (GLN21 and BLN16) to establish foundational detection capabilities. Subsequently, we conducted four consecutive rounds of uncertainty-driven refinement (Iterations 2–5). In each round, the model performed inference on the unlabeled candidate pool to compute tile-level uncertainty scores      u    i      (derived from the uncertainty module). WSIs were then prioritized for expert review according to a slide-level diagnostic ambiguity score. Specifically, for a given WSI with N tiles, we defined ambiguity as the mean uncertainty of the top K most uncertain tiles:   9    A   (   W  S  I   )   =    1    K      ∑    i  ϵ  T  o  p  −  K      u    i    ,  K  =   ⌈   0.05  ⋅  N   ⌉      Here,     Top  −  K     denotes the set of tiles with the largest uncertainty scores within that WSI, and ┌.┐ is the ceiling operator. WSIs were ranked by     A     WSI        in descending order and selected for pathologist review.  Specifically, the top 200 WSIs were selected in iterations 2 and 3, while the top 100 WSIs were selected in iterations 4 and 5. Senior pathologists reviewed these flagged samples to correct FPs and verify missed metastases. After each review phase, the corrected samples were incorporated into the expanded training set.    Data annotation and establishment of ground truth  To satisfy the distinct requirements of model development and independent validation, we implemented a two-tier annotation strategy conducted by senior pathologists with over 15 years of experience (Y.C., C.Q., J.L., C.B., and M.S.).  For the development cohort, pathologists performed exhaustive region-level annotations on WSIs selected for the expanded training set and the internal validation set. This involved delineating precise boundaries for all LNs and contouring all internal metastatic foci. This process ensured that the model received high-granularity supervision for distinct metastatic morphologies, including macro-metastases, micro-metastases, and isolated tumor cells (ITCs). During active learning iterations, regions flagged as HU were specifically reviewed and corrected (C.Q., J.L., C.B., and M.S.) to provide high-quality supervision for challenging examples.  For the independent test cohort, we established a rigorous diagnostic standard to evaluate clinical safety. Instead of pixel-level contours, we focused on the definitive metastatic status of each LN. Two senior pathologists (Y.C. and C.Q.) independently reviewed all WSIs. Discrepant cases were adjudicated by a consensus panel. To resolve diagnostic ambiguity in morphologically challenging cases, we performed confirmatory immunohistochemical (IHC) staining (CAM5.2 and AE1/AE3) on 52 challenging cases to determine the final ground truth (SFig.  12 ). This process ensured a non-ambiguous “Positive/Negative” label for every LN in the test set.    Statistical analysis  The detection (YOLOv8-s) and segmentation (nnUNet) models were implemented with probability thresholds of 0.25 and 0.50, respectively. For the classification model, the binary decision threshold was set at 0.50. The uncertainty threshold for each iteration was determined empirically using the Internal Validation Set. To balance the trade-off between the volume of regions flagged for review and FP predictions, we selected the threshold at the intersection point where the average High Uncertainty area per slide (HUavg) equalled the average False Positive area per slide (FPavg) (SFig.  13 ). Isolated positive predictions approximately the size of one tile (3600 μm²) were excluded from analysis owing to resolution constraints.  To comprehensively evaluate the system, we defined detection and classification targets at three distinct levels. Tile-level performance measures the fundamental classification accuracy of individual 256 × 256 pixel image patches, where a tile is labeled positive if tumor tissue comprises >25% of its area. Lesion-level (Region) performance evaluates the model’s ability to correctly localize and classify contiguous metastatic areas (including macro-metastases, micro-metastases, and ITCs) within the LN tissue, distinct from simple tile-level accuracy. LN-level performance serves as the primary clinical unit for N-staging; an LN is considered positive if the model identifies at least one metastatic lesion within the nodal area.  We defined specific metrics to assess the safety and efficiency of the proposed human-AI collaborative workflow. Conditional classification sensitivity evaluates the classification performance specifically on all LNs successfully localized by the detection module. For performance evaluation, regions flagged as HU (highlighted in yellow in the prediction heatmaps) were considered positive for sensitivity calculations, as these areas require pathologist review in clinical practice. To quantify workload, we defined the Review Burden Rate on Negative Cases (RBR-N) as the proportion of true-negative LNs that required high-magnification manual review. An LN contributes to this burden if it contains any region predicted as False Positive (FP) or High Uncertainty (HU).  Bootstrap analysis (1000 iterations) was performed to calculate 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for all performance metrics. AUCs were compared using DeLong’s test (two-sided). evidence_text: Artificial Intelligence in Orthopedic Surgery: Current Applications, Challenges, and Future Directions. Artificial intelligence (AI) drives transformative changes in orthopedic surgery, steering it toward precision and personalization through intelligent applications in preoperative planning, intraoperative assistance, and postoperative rehabilitation/monitoring. Breakthroughs in deep learning, robotics, and multimodal data fusion have enabled AI to demonstrate significant advantages. Nonetheless, current applications face challenges such as limited real-time decision autonomy, fragmented medical data silos, standardization gaps restricting model generalization, and ethical/regulatory frameworks lagging behind technological advancements. Therefore, a critical analysis of the current status of AI and the acceleration of its clinical translation is urgently required. This study systematically reviews the core advancements, challenges, and future directions of AI in orthopedic surgery from technical, clinical, and ethical perspectives. It elaborates on the "perceptual-decisional-executional" intelligent closed loop formed by algorithmic innovation and hardware upgrades, summarizes AI applications across surgical continuum, analyzes ethical and regulatory challenges, and explores emerging trajectories. This review integrates the end-to-end applications of AI in orthopedics, illustrating its evolution. It introduces an "algorithm-hardware-ethics trinity" framework for technical translation, providing methodological guidance for interdisciplinary collaboration. Additionally, it evaluates the combined efficacy of diverse algorithms and devices through practical cases and details of future research frontiers, aiming to inform researchers of current landscapes and guide subsequent investigations.

evidence_text:
Gut microbiota preserves bone mass through modulating the hyodeoxycholic acid-TGR5 axis.

Background

Osteoporosis is an age-related disease. The relationship between gut microbiota (GM) homeostasis and bone health is well established, but the mechanism of GM dysbiosis contributes to senile osteoporosis remains elusive. The objective of this study is to investigate the relationship between GM, bile acids (BAs) and their effects on bone mass.

Results

16S rRNA sequencing and untargeted and targeted metabolomics revealed a reduction in microbial diversity, accompanied by the change of BA profile. In particular, the abundance of Parabacteroides goldsteinii and hyodeoxycholic acid (HDCA) in old mice were markedly decreased, compared with young mice. And there was a strong positive correlation between the abundance of P. goldsteinii and HDCA and bone mass. Further, our results demonstrated that old mice cohoused with young mice, with/without coprophagy prevention, were unable to alter the GM composition or reverse age-related bone loss. The transplantation of GM from young mice into old mice, rather than the transplantation of P. goldsteinii alone, reconstructed the GM of old mice and preserved bone mass by inhibiting bone resorption. Mechanistically, HDCA inhibits osteoclast maturation in vitro and exerts the bone protection effect in vivo through the activation of the G protein-coupled bile acid receptor (TGR5). HDCA treatment has been shown to result in the internalization of TGR5, thereby inhibiting the nuclear translocation of P65 in vivo. Knockout of TGR5 attenuated the effects of HDCA on bone microstructure, confirming these findings.

Conclusions

This study identified the GM-HDCA-TGR5 axis is a key pathway that affects bone mass and targeted intervention of HDCA represents potential therapeutic option for osteoporosis.

title: ChromBERT: A foundation model for learning interpretable representations for context-specific transcriptional regulatory networks.

evidence_text: ChromBERT: A foundation model for learning interpretable representations for context-specific transcriptional regulatory networks. Gene expression is shaped by transcriptional regulatory networks (TRNs), where transcription regulators interact within regulatory elements in a context-specific manner. Deciphering context-specific TRNs has long been constrained by the severe sparsity of cell-type-specific chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) profiles. Here, we present ChromBERT, a foundation model pre-trained on large-scale human ChIP-seq datasets covering ∼1,000 transcription regulators. ChromBERT learns the genome-wide syntax of regulatory cooperation and generates interpretable TRN representations. After prompt-enhanced fine-tuning, it outperforms existing methods for imputing unseen cistromes. Moreover, lightweight fine-tuning on cell-type-specific downstream tasks adapts the TRN representations to capture regulatory effects and dynamics within any given cellular context. The resulting context-specific representations can then be interpreted to infer regulatory roles of transcription regulators underlying these cell-type-specific regulatory outcomes without requiring additional ChIP-seq experiments. By overcoming the limitations of sparse transcription regulator data, ChromBERT significantly enhances our ability to model and interpret transcriptional regulation across a wide range of biological contexts.

title: Enhancing antibody-antigen interaction prediction with atomic flexibility.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: Enhancing antibody-antigen interaction prediction with atomic flexibility. Antibodies are indispensable components of the immune system, known for their specific binding to antigens. Beyond their natural immunological functions, they are fundamental in developing vaccines and therapeutic interventions for infectious diseases. The complex architecture of antibodies, particularly their variable regions responsible for antigen recognition, presents significant challenges for computational modeling. Recent advancements in deep learning have markedly improved protein structure prediction; however, accurately modeling antibody-antigen (Ab-Ag) interactions remains challenging due to the inherent flexibility of antibodies and the dynamic nature of binding processes. In this study, we examine the use of predicted Local Distance Difference Test (pLDDT) scores as indicators of residue and side-chain flexibility to model Ab-Ag interactions through a fingerprint-based approach. We demonstrate the significance of flexibility in different antibody-specific tasks, enhancing the predictive accuracy of Ab-Ag interaction models by 4%, resulting in an AUC-ROC of 92%. In addition, we showcase state-of-the-art performance in paratope prediction. These results emphasize the importance of accounting for conformational flexibility in modeling antibody-antigen interactions and show that pLDDT can serve as a coarse proxy for these dynamic features. By optimizing antibody flexibility using pLDDT, they can be engineered to improve affinity or breadth for a specific target. This approach is particularly beneficial for addressing highly variable pathogens like HIV and SARS-CoV-2, as greater flexibility enhances tolerance to sequence variations in target antigens.

evidence_text: The Augmented Cytopathologist: A Conceptual Exploratory Narrative Review on Immersive and Vision-Language Models Tools in Digital Pathology. Emerging digital technologies, including immersive environments (VR/AR/XR) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), have the potential to reshape digital pathology and medical imaging. While immersive tools can enhance spatial visualization and procedural training, VLM-based copilots offer cognitive and workflow support. Their combined impact on cytopathology remains largely conceptual and preclinical. This Conceptual Exploratory Narrative Review (CENR) examines how immersive technologies and VLM-based copilots may jointly influence cytopathologists' professional workflow, training, and diagnostic processes, introducing the notion of the "augmented cytopathologist." A structured exploratory approach integrated peer-reviewed literature, position papers, preprints, gray literature (technical reports, white papers, conference abstracts, blogs), and cross-disciplinary perspectives. Background

Pneumoconioses remain an important occupational health issue, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. The International Labour Organization (ILO) Classification standardizes chest radiograph interpretation but requires trained readers and is affected by inter-reader variability. This study evaluated whether generative multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) models can approximate ILO-based diagnostic reasoning.

Methods

Eighty-two chest radiographs from the official NIOSH B Reader syllabus were analysed using four AI systems (GPT-4o, GPT-5, MedGemma-4B, MedGemma-27B). Each image was evaluated with a standardized prompt based on the 2022 revised ILO guidelines using deterministic settings. Model outputs were mapped to ILO codes and compared with the official answer keys of the ILO Standard Radiograph Set used for B Reader training and examination. Performance metrics included balanced accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC). Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, McNemar's test, and Cohen's κ assessed performance variability and agreement.

Results

All four AI models showed moderate diagnostic performance, with balanced accuracy ranging from 60.8% to 70.3%. Sensitivity remained limited (35.5%-54.9%), while specificity was consistently high (84.6%-86.2%). MedGemma-27B performed best for small opacities, GPT-5 for pleural abnormalities and for technical quality. Large opacities and rare findings were systematically under-detected. Statistical comparisons showed significant differences between models, although agreement patterns were broadly similar.

Conclusion

All AI models partially followed structured ILO radiographic criteria but did not achieve expert-level performance, confirming that they cannot replace certified B Readers. Larger, real-world datasets are needed to assess their potential clinical utility as supportive tools in occupational health surveillance programs.

evidence_text: Impact of tissue staining and scanner variation on the performance of pathology foundation models: a study of sarcomas and their mimics Histopathological analysis is considered the gold standard for the diagnosis and prognostication of cancer. Recent advances in AI, driven by large-scale digitisation and pan-cancer foundation models, are opening new opportunities for clinical integration. However, it remains unclear how robust these foundation models are to real-world sources of variability, particularly in H&E staining and scanning protocols. In this study, we use soft tissue tumours, a rare and morphologically diverse tumour type, as a challenging test case to systematically investigate the colour-related robustness and generalisability of seven AI models. Controlled staining and scanning experiments were utilised to assess model performance across diverse real-world data sources. Foundation models, particularly UNI-v2, Virchow and TITAN, demonstrated encouraging robustness to staining and scanning variation, particularly when a small number of stain-varied slides were included in the training loop, highlighting their potential as adaptable and data-efficient tools for real-world digital pathology workflows.

evidence_text: Intelligent Support for Radiotherapy: A Review of Clinical Applications for Large Language Models. Background: Radiotherapy (RT) is a core modality for cancer treatment, yet it is plagued by inter-observer variability in target delineation, inefficient manual workflows, and challenges in fusing multi-type clinical data. Large language models (LLMs), with their superior semantic understanding and cross-modal fusion capabilities present novel solutions to these challenges. Scope: This narrative review provided a comprehensive overview of the current landscape and emerging trends of LLM applications across the entire RT workflow. Findings: LLMs demonstrated substantial clinical utility in key RT domains, including automated target volume delineation (e.g., Medformer, Radformer), dose prediction (e.g., DoseGNN), treatment planning automation (e.g., GPT-Plan), patient education, clinical decision support, medical information extraction, and prognosis assessment. These applications not only have the potential to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of RT but also facilitate the standardization of clinical pathways. However, widespread clinical adoption was impeded by critical limitations, including model hallucinations, insufficient generalizability, and unresolved issues regarding data privacy and ethical governance. Conclusions: LLMs possessed transformative potential to revolutionize radiation oncology. Future endeavors should prioritize technical refinements to mitigate model deficiencies, establish standardized evaluation benchmarks, and develop robust ethical frameworks. These concerted efforts are crucial for translating LLM research into clinical practice and advancing the era of intelligent, precision RT.

evidence_text: Vision-Enabled AI scribes reduce omissions in clinical conversations: evidence from simulated medication histories. Most ambient AI medical scribes process audio only, omitting clinically important visual details. We developed a vision-enabled AI scribe using Google's Gemini model and Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses to document medication histories-a task requiring both audio and visual input. Ten clinical pharmacists video-recorded 110 simulated medication history interviews. Following iterative prompt engineering on 10 training recordings, the scribe was evaluated on 100 test recordings (2160 data points) across patient details and medication-specific fields. The vision-enabled scribe achieved 98% overall accuracy (2114/2,160 data points), ranging from 96% for patient details to 99% for dosing directions and indication. Video input significantly outperformed audio-only processing (98% vs 81%, P < 0.001), primarily through reduced omissions (10 vs 358 errors). Vision-enabled AI scribes substantially improved documentation accuracy for tasks requiring visual input, demonstrating potential to markedly reduce omission errors in clinical documentation.

evidence_text: Fragment-based discovery of TopBP1 inhibitors integrated with AI-driven molecular docking. DNA topoisomerase IIβ-binding protein 1 (TopBP1) converges on multiple oncogenic pathways, e.g., Rb, p53, and PI3K/Akt, which are hallmarks of most cancer progression. However, the lack of structural studies makes the underlying mechanism of action of TopBP1 inhibitors promiscuous. Herein, we employ a fragment-based screening approach to identify four small-molecule ligands against the TopBP1 BRCT7-8 domain: adamantane acetic acid (ADA), zaltoprofen, diclofenac sodium, and quinine. The dissociation constants of these compounds are determined by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) chemical shift perturbations, which suggests the former three hits bind to the same site, while quinine binds to a distinct site. The binding models of these four hits are further predicted by the deep learning model Chai-1. The complex crystal structure of the TopBP1 BRCT7-8 domain demonstrates ADA as an orthosteric inhibitor of TopBP1, as further validated by its binding to TopBP1 in competition with the native substrate BACH1. Our NMR screening nominates orthosteric inhibitors, as well as quinine, a potential allosteric inhibitor. It shall also facilitate following structure-based design of more potent allosteric and orthosteric inhibitors of TopBP1.

title: New approach methodologies for drug discovery.

evidence_text: New approach methodologies for drug discovery. Traditional animal-based drug discovery has high failure rates, prompting the search for and adoption of human-centered new approach methodologies (NAMs). Rapid advances in stem cell-, organoid-, and in silico-based NAMs, supported by evolving frameworks from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), now span the entire drug-discovery continuum, from disease modeling and drug design to efficacy testing. Our review highlights recent progress across these domains, including the identification of therapeutic candidates, the development of cutting-edge models and technologies, and the potential of NAMs themselves as treatments in preclinical and clinical contexts, while examining the key biological, technical, and regulatory bottlenecks that need to be addressed to enable robust translational adoption. We conclude by discussing the translational and societal considerations essential to the responsible adoption of NAMs and outlining future human-centric pipelines poised to redefine the landscape of drug discovery.

evidence_text:
Graphicalized vision-language modeling for comprehensive lung nodule analysis and risk stratification. Lung cancer care involves coupled tasks such as precise nodule detection, patient-level survival risk estimation, and nodule count quantification, typically handled by separate systems despite clear interdependence. We present VITALIS, a multimodal vision-language framework that fuses CT and PET/CT imaging with structured radiology text using a graph-aware Transformer: Laplacian diffusion enriches token features on an image-text graph, while structural and prior-guided attention focus computation on anatomically and clinically related contexts, followed by bidirectional image-text conditioning to form a fused patient representation. This representation parameterizes a continuous-time latent risk process governed by a context-modulated Neural ODE, enabling individualized continuous-time modeling of time-to-event risk. Task-specific heads decode the latent trajectory into nodule detection, nodule malignancy classification, survival risk estimation, and nodule count prediction. Evaluated on three public cohorts, the framework delivers accurate delineations, low-false-positive localization, calibrated survival risk estimates, and consistent nodule counts across tasks. These findings indicate that coupling graph-aware multimodal encoding with continuous-time latent dynamics provides a coherent basis for integrated diagnostic and prognostic modeling in lung cancer. Introduction  Lung cancer diagnosis and management require several critical tasks, including the detection of suspicious pulmonary nodules, prognostic survival prediction for patients, and estimation of nodule count as an index of nodule burden. Precise delineation of nodule boundaries is essential for treatment planning and disease monitoring  1 , 2  , while early nodule detection via low-dose CT screening has been shown to significantly reduce lung cancer mortality  3  . In parallel, reliable survival prediction can inform personalized therapy and follow-up intensity, and quantifying the number of nodules aids in risk stratification and staging.  VITALIS  is proposed as a unified multimodal framework to address these needs by concurrently performing lung nodule detection, malignancy classification, survival risk estimation, and nodule count prediction within a single model. This integrated approach is motivated by the potential to streamline clinical workflows: enabling comprehensive analysis of imaging and clinical data in one pass, and to exploit synergies between tasks.  Several recent studies have explored advanced deep learning methods for lung nodule detection and nodule segmentation. Zhou et al.  1   introduced a multitask connected U-Net with a teacher-student architecture that integrates PET and CT data to improve automated lung nodule segmentation, leveraging PET-derived knowledge to guide more precise CT-based contouring. Cai et al.  4   developed MSDet, a multiscale attention network with an extended receptive field and specialized modules for tiny-objects to improve the detection of very small pulmonary nodules on CT scans. Tang et al.  5   proposed an anchor-free detector called Circle-YOLO, which represents lung nodules with bounding circles and employs a novel attention mechanism to localize nodules without preset anchor boxes. Niu et al.  3   presented a large-scale foundation model (M3FM) for lung cancer screening that uses a synergistic multimodal, multitask transformer architecture to handle multiple screening tasks end-to-end.  Other works have focused on prognostic modeling and multimodal data integration for lung cancer outcomes. Mikhael et al.  6   developed the Sybil model, a deep learning approach that analyzes a single low-dose CT scan without any manual annotations or added clinical data to predict an individual’s 1–6 year lung cancer risk. Kanakarajan et al.  7   built an ensemble predictive model that combines clinical variables, engineered radiomic features, and deep learning representations from CT images to estimate overall survival in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients. Zhang et al.  8   applied deep learning to histopathology slides, using contrastive clustering on H&E-stained tissue images to discover prognostic morphologic phenotypes and predict patient outcomes in small cell lung cancer. Salmanpour et al.  9   proposed a semi-supervised framework for lung cancer survival prediction that leverages pseudo-labeling and diverse multicenter PET/CT datasets to improve model generalization in outcome prediction. Liao et al.  10   integrated advanced intratumoral and peritumoral radiomic features with clinical parameters in a DeepSurv model to personalize immunotherapy response prediction for lung cancer patients, demonstrating the value of combined imaging and clinical data for outcome modeling. Amaro et al.  11   explored convolutional neural network approaches using CT scans to extract prognostic information, comparing multiple CNN architectures for their efficacy in predicting survival of lung cancer patients  12  .  Each of these studies addresses a piece of the lung cancer prediction puzzle in detection, or risk prediction, and underscores the need for a comprehensive system like VITALIS that can tackle all these aspects together.    Results  The evaluation of the VITALIS framework was designed to comprehensively assess both its overall performance and the specific contributions of its architectural components. To this end, we benchmarked VITALIS against a diverse set of state-of-the-art methods across four complementary tasks. The analysis begins with core spatial localization capabilities (detection), extends to higher-level prognostic objectives (risk prediction and nodule count estimation), and concludes with an ablation study that isolates and quantifies the impact of each model module. All data used in this study were obtained exclusively from the datasets listed in Table  7 .    Table 7   Summary of public datasets for model development and validation      Collection name  Size  Modalities  Annotation/Ground truth      LIDC-IDRI  1018 cases  Thoracic CT  Radiologist segmentations    LUNG-PET-CT-DX  355 subjects  CT, PET (PET/CT)  Tissue histopathological diagnosis and bounding boxes (XML)    ACRIN-NSCLC-FDG-PET (ACRIN 6668)  242 subjects  Serial FDG-PET/CT  Clinical outcome data (survival, tumor response)       Lung nodule detection  The performance of the model was quantified using the standard object detection metrics of Precision (positive predictive value) and Recall (sensitivity). The F1-score (F1) is reported as the harmonic mean of these two, providing a single, balanced measure of overall detection accuracy. And the average number of false positives per scan (FP/s) is included as the primary metric for clinical viability.  All detection results reported correspond to a confidence threshold of 0.5 for classifying a candidate as a nodule. This threshold was chosen on each dataset’s validation set to maximize the F1-score, thereby balancing sensitivity and precision for optimal low-false-positive performance. We found the model’s performance to be robust with respect to this choice: varying the threshold by ±0.1 yielded only minor changes in precision/recall (on the order of 1–2%) and did not alter the relative ranking of methods. This insensitivity indicates that our reported low false-positive rates are not a tuning artifact but rather an inherent strength of the VITALIS detector.  As detailed in Table  1 , the VITALIS framework unequivocally outperforms all competing models on both benchmark datasets: LIDC-IDRI cohort and Lung-PET-CT-Dx cohort. One finding from Table  1  is the model’s ability to achieve high sensitivity while maintaining an exceptionally low false-positive rate. On the LIDC-IDRI dataset, VITALIS achieves a 91.09% F1-score with only 0.39 FP/s. This represents a 2.12-point F1 improvement over the next-best model, LN-Detr (88.97% F1), while simultaneously reducing the false-positive rate by 18.8% (from 0.48 FP/s).  This trend is even more pronounced on the more complex, multimodal Lung-PET-CT-Dx dataset. VITALIS achieves a 93.55% F1-score at a remarkably low 0.29 FP/s. For comparison, the next best Circle-YOLO  5   reaches only 89.98% F1 and incurs 40% more false positives (0.48 FP/s). This simultaneous optimization suggests that the model’s enriched, multimodal feature representation provides a highly discriminative feature space. This allows the model to confidently reject challenging false-positive cases.    Survival risk prediction  For the task of 2-year lung cancer survival risk prediction, we evaluate model performance using both discrimination and calibration metrics. Discriminative ability is quantified by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and the concordance index (C-index), which both measure how well the model’s risk scores differentiate patients with different outcomes. Calibration and overall predictive accuracy are assessed via the Brier score (mean squared error of probability forecasts; here reported as a percentage, with lower values indicating more accurate, calibrated risk predictions). In addition to these continuous measures, we examine binary classification performance at the clinically relevant 2-year survival threshold: specifically, we compute the precision, recall (sensitivity), and  F  1 -score for classifying patients as having survived at least 2 years or not, based on the risk estimate.  Table  2  presents the survival prediction results on the ACRIN 6668 dataset. VITALIS achieves an AUC of about 0.869 and a C-index of 0.860, which are the highest among the methods compared. In particular, the AUC is roughly 1.7–1.9 points higher in absolute terms than the strongest prior model (which attains ~0.85), indicating a meaningful improvement in the model’s ability to distinguish high-risk versus low-risk patients. This suggests that the integration of multimodal imaging and clinical text by VITALIS yields more informative risk stratification than models using imaging or clinical data alone. VITALIS has the lowest Brier score, outperforming competing approaches, which often have Brier scores in the 16–19 range. This lower Brier score signifies that the probabilistic risk estimates from VITALIS are better calibrated and more accurate on an absolute scale, reflecting improved reliability in its predictions. From a clinical decision point of view, this means that VITALIS not only separates patients by outcome more effectively, but also provides risk probabilities that better reflect true outcome frequencies.  At the binary 2-year survival endpoint, VITALIS likewise achieves superior results. It achieves an  F  1 -score of about 0.81. Both precision and recall for the positive class are improved relative to alternatives, indicating that VITALIS catches a greater portion of truly high-risk patients (few false negatives) while also making fewer incorrect high-risk predictions (few false positives). This balanced improvement in precision and recall underscores the model’s practical utility: it can identify those at risk of 2-year mortality more accurately, which is crucial for guiding timely interventions, without unduly overestimating risk for lower-risk patients. In summary, the risk prediction results demonstrate that VITALIS provides a markedly better combination of discrimination and calibration than existing methods. The model’s use of longitudinal latent dynamics and multimodal data appears to capture subtle prognostic patterns that enable more precise survival risk estimation.    Trajectory plausibility  To verify that the learned continuous-time latent representations genuinely reflect physiological disease progression, we evaluated trajectory plausibility on the ACRIN 6668 paired-scan subset. For VITALIS, we compared the Neural ODE-predicted latent state at the follow-up time against the actual encoded post-treatment scan. For static baseline models, we approximated future states using linear feature extrapolation. To comprehensively assess representation fidelity, we utilized three complementary topological metrics: Cosine Similarity evaluates the semantic alignment based on the direction the latent vectors point, invariant to their magnitude; Normalized  ℓ  2  distance quantifies the absolute spatial proximity and structural dissimilarity within the representation manifold; and Directional Agreement captures the angular consistency between the inferred and true progression velocities, ensuring the modeled path correctly tracks actual biological changes. As illustrated in Fig.  1 . VITALIS effectively captures longitudinal disease dynamics, maintaining high directional agreement and semantic consistency (high cosine similarity, low normalized  ℓ  2  distance). In contrast, the representations of static baseline models exhibit severe semantic drift over time, confirming the necessity of explicit continuous-time dynamics modeling.    Fig. 1   Trajectory plausibility diagnostics.  Bar plots comparing trajectory fidelity across models using three complementary metrics: Cosine Similarity, Normalized ℓ2 distance, and Directional Agreement.                     Malignancy classification  To ensure rigorous validation and direct comparability with contemporary state-of-the-art literature, we utilized the LIDC-IDRI dataset for all malignancy classification experiments. The LIDC-IDRI dataset provides malignancy ratings from four blinded radiologists on an ordinal scale of 1–5. Benign (Negative Class): Nodules with an average malignancy rating <3 (combining “Highly Unlikely” and “Moderately Unlikely”). Malignant (Positive Class): Nodules with an average malignancy rating >3 (combining “Moderately Suspicious” and “Highly Suspicious”). Exclusion Criteria: Nodules with an indeterminate average rating of exactly 3 were excluded to minimize label noise and ensure the model learns robust, definitive features of malignancy. This rigorous partitioning ensures that all nodules belonging to a single patient are strictly segregated into either the training or the testing fold, thereby eliminating the risk of data leakage via patient-specific imaging artifacts. Discussion  In this work, we propose VITALIS, a multimodal deep learning framework that integrates four core tasks of lung cancer care, including nodule detection, survival risk prediction, and nodule count estimation. Using the architectural construct and multimodality of VITALIS provides learning synergism for all tasks. A shared feature encoder (derived from image and clinical inputs) is associated with task-specific prediction heads to enable shared nodule features to produce different outcomes. The detection elements of the model learn in-depth features of nodules and masses from radiography and give informative labels that are also relevant for the survival prediction head. This multitask architecture not only expedites (diagnosis and prognosis can be generated in one model), but it also helps to promote data transfer between tasks so that overall robustness is better. Training on varied data modalities—say, medical image together with patient metadata or textual reports VITALIS takes advantage of complementary data that single-modality models may miss. Clinical context (e.g., patient demographics or pathology findings, if available), together with imaging data, enables the model to enhance risk assessments and count estimates by accounting for a better, more comprehensive view of the disease condition.  Methodologically, VITALIS shows the possibility of a model that uses a single predictor for lung cancer. Our model can solve practical concerns in the sense that it generates nodule detection and patient-level risk indices within the same framework, obviating the need for a separate system. Joint training of these objectives is used as a regularization; it needs to discover latent representations that can provide detection of visible lesions and prediction of clinical outcomes, thus leading to more generalized feature learning. Based on the performance metrics and experimental results we provide for specific tasks, this ensemble strategy can provide more stable and reliable results for tasks. Instruments are even now available to count the detected nodules within a particular network for quantification of nodule burden, and this may be useful in clinic-based staging and for the prediction of disease progression over time.  In conclusion, VITALIS contributes to advancing multimodal modeling for comprehensive lung cancer analysis. Its multimodal, multitask design embodies a shift from task-specific algorithms to an integrated decision-support system. Such a system can potentially improve efficiency (by consolidating inferencing) and consistency (by using the same underlying data representation for all predictions) in clinical practice. While careful prospective validation and refinement are needed before deployment, especially to ensure generalization across different institutions and imaging protocols, the present study’s findings underscore the viability of a unified model addressing both diagnostic and prognostic aspects of lung cancer. A limitation is the interpretability of intermediate continuous-time latent states when longitudinal ground truth is sparse. The Ergodic Progression Hypothesis (EPH) is used as a modeling viewpoint to connect cohort heterogeneity with within-patient progression.    Methods  We introduce VITALIS (Variational Graph-Attentive Transformer with Latent ODEs), shown in Fig.  5 , a multimodal vision language model for lung cancer prediction. The architecture consists of three components : (1) a context encoder that processes imaging and textual inputs (CT scans, PET scans, and structured radiology annotations) with a graph-aware Transformer, producing a fused patient context vector  c ; (2) a continuous-time latent dynamics module (Neural ODE  17  ) that evolves a personalized latent state  z ( t ) under an ODE defined by the context  c ; and (3) multitask observation heads that map the latent trajectory  z ( t ) to clinically relevant outputs (nodule detection, malignancy classification, risk estimation, and nodule count). The entire model is trained end-to-end with the adjoint sensitivity method for the ODE, incorporating spectral regularization.
