The first two terms minimize transcriptomic and morphological discrepancies between the iteratively aligned source and target, weighted by the matching probability       . The final term regularizes        in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, ensuring smooth and invertible mappings [ 36 ]. The selected        gene channels and histological image channel act as alignment ‘landmarks’, guiding the optimization—principally differing from STalign, which does not utilize this information. Additional details are provided in  Supplementary Section S1.2 .  We adopt a coupled optimization strategy that jointly refines GA alignment and local diffeomorphic deformation within a unified objective. In the global stage, a genetic algorithm (GA) [ 37 ] conducts a population-based search to estimate affine parameters and overlapping regions, providing robust initialization that avoids local minima. Subsequently, the local stage resolves residual nonlinear discrepancies using large deformation diffeomorphic metric mapping (LDDMM) [ 36 ], modelling smooth, invertible deformations suitable for fine-grained spatial adjustments. To reconcile local deformations with modality-specific information, an EM-like LDDMM scheme is implemented: in the E-step, matching probabilities        are updated from current residual kernels; in the M-step, the velocity field        is optimized by minimizing the weighted quadratic registration energy under the LDDMM framework, while        is updated accordingly. The pseudo-code of GALA is provided in  Supplementary Algorithm S1 .  Unlike conventional pipelines that perform global (coarse) and local (fine) alignment independently, our coordinated coarse-to-fine scheme iteratively reinforces both stages. This bidirectional coupling, where coarse estimates guide local refinements and local updates feedback to adjust global parameters, enables more stable convergence than purely hierarchical or decoupled approaches. A full mathematical formulation and optimization procedure are provided in  Supplementary Section 1.3 . Empirically, under default parameter settings ( Supplementary Table S1 ), only two global–local episodes suffice to achieve stable alignment across most datasets ( Supplementary Fig. S3 ).  Selection of informative genes and hyper-parameters  GALA requires two key hyper-parameters: the number of selected informative genes       , which guide alignment, and the relative weight        that balances contributions from transcriptomics profiles versus histological images.  For gene selection, we adopted the       -based strategy from GPSA [ 21 ], which ranks genes by their predictability from local spatial context. Specifically, for each gene, a       -nearest neighbour (      NN) regression model is trained to predict expression levels from the spatial coordinates of neighbouring spots or cells. The coefficient of determination (      ) quantifies spatial predictability, and the top        genes with the highest        values from the source data are retained. Detailed robustness and sensitivity analyses, as well as spatial coverage analysis of informative genes, are provided in  Supplementary Sections S2.1.1, S2.1.2, and S2.1.4 .    Evaluation metrics  To evaluate alignment performance across diverse experimental scenarios, we employ complementary metrics capturing spatial accuracy, biological coherence, and molecular consistency. Metrics are selected based on dataset characteristics, such as availability of anatomical annotations, spatial resolution, and modality, to ensure biologically meaningful and context-appropriate assessment.  When anatomical labels or ground truth are available, we assess alignment fidelity using two strategies. First, label consistency accuracy identifies mutual nearest-neighbour pairs between aligned slices and reports the proportion sharing the same anatomical label, directly quantifying structural correspondence and, more specifically, the preservation of biologically defined regions [ 8 ]. Second, biological coherence is evaluated via clustering-based metrics: a joint Gaussian mixture module (GMM) is fitted to combined spatial and gene expression features from both aligned source and target slices, and cluster assignments are compared with ground-truth labels using adjusted Rand index (ARI) and normalized mutual information (NMI). These metrics assess how well alignment preserves region-specific transcriptional and anatomical structure.  For spot-based datasets lacking reliable anatomical annotations, spatial cross-correlation metrics quantify preservation of continuous spatial gene expression gradients [ 40 ,  41 ]. For each gene, correlations between transcriptomic profiles in aligned source and target slices are computed with Gaussian-kernel weights based on inter-spot distances. Averaging across genes provides a global measure of spatial expression consistency, capturing local gradient preservation without requiring labels. Further details on evaluation metrics are provided in  Supplementary Section S1.4 .  In cell-based datasets, direct cell-to-cell comparison is often unreliable due to biological heterogeneity and measurement sparsity. Following STalign [ 12 ], neighbouring cells are aggregated into pseudo-spots to stabilize expression signals. Cosine similarity between corresponding pseudo-spots across aligned slices then quantifies local molecular agreement, mitigating single-cell noise, and providing an effective fidelity measure for high-resolution single-cell datasets without histological or anatomical ground truth.  For transcriptomics-to-histology alignment, we use the mean absolute error (MAE) of annotated landmark coordinates:        where        indexes landmarks, and        denote the coordinates of the       th landmark in the target and aligned source data, respectively. Lower MAE indicates better spatial correspondence and provides an evaluation that is independent of gene expression or clustering assumptions, making it compatible with landmark-free alignment methods.  Overall, each metric is selected to match the characteristics of the corresponding dataset and alignment task, capturing structural correspondence (label consistency, MAE), transcriptional coherence (ARI, NMI, and pseudo-spot similarity), or preservation of spatial expression gradients (cross-correlation). These quantitative measures are complemented by visual overlays of aligned slices, providing intuitive verification of spot/cell correspondence, gene expression patterns, and regional morphology. Together, they offer a comprehensive assessment of GALA’s performance across diverse ST datasets.    Implementation techniques for all alignment scenarios  GALA is a versatile alignment framework applicable to widespread application scenarios (see  Fig. 1c ). For example, whether the source and target data (i) belong to the same modality or not, (ii) are consistent in spatial resolution or not, and (iii) are fully or partially overlapped. In the following, we detail how GALA is applied across these scenarios.  First, because rasterization maps each dataset onto a user-defined grid, same-modality alignment under both matched and mismatched resolutions, including spot-to-spot, cell-to-cell, and cell-to-spot scenarios, is handled directly through the choice of grid spacing        (see Section Data preprocessing and rasterization). No additional algorithmic modifications are required: once rasterized, all datasets are processed identically by the optimization pipeline. This design enables resolution-aware and platform-agnostic alignment across Visium, Xenium, MERFISH, and related technologies.  Second, GALA supports cross-modality alignment, such as registering ST measurements to histological images from the same tissue section. Histology images are converted to greyscale and transformed into structural contrast maps, whereas transcriptomic measurements are encoded as rasterization tensors, allowing both to be treated as image-like modalities. Alignment is then performed under the multimodal objective:        where        and       . This variant enables cross-modality alignment without requiring landmarks or manual correspondence, facilitating integration across different types of measurements in ST studies.  Third, GALA explicitly accommodates partial alignment. The framework first performs a population-based affine parameter search to approximate the overlapping region between the two datasets. This GA estimate then guides the subsequent LDDMM-based refinement. During refinement, an EM-like procedure updates pixel-wise correspondence weights, allowing the model to concentrate on structurally matched areas while downweighting unmatched or noisy areas (see Section Alignment objective and optimization). This mechanism confers robustness in scenarios involving incomplete, distorted, or physically damaged tissue.  Finally, GALA’s multimodal rasterization and flexible objective function allow natural extension to other omics modalities beyond transcriptomics. For instance, metabolic or proteomic imaging data can be rasterized similarly, enabling alignment of metabolite distributions or protein expression patterns to transcriptomic or histological references. This generalizability makes GALA a broadly applicable framework for multi-omics spatial alignment, supporting integrative studies across diverse molecular modalities and imaging platforms. Landmark selection is inherently subjective and prone to user bias. Different experts may select different landmarks, leading to inconsistent alignments. For instance, when landmarks are sparse or lack anatomical specificity, STalign’s performance degrades markedly ( Supplementary Fig. S15 ). In contrast, GALA does not rely on manual landmarks during optimization, eliminating user bias, and ensuring fully data-driven alignment. Landmarks are used only for independent evaluation, with a larger set of points than those provided to STalign, allowing an objective and fair comparison of geometric consistency across methods. This separation between optimization and evaluation allows GALA to remain fully automated and reproducible, while still enabling an objective assessment of alignment quality.    Computational efficiency  All methods were benchmarked under consistent hardware conditions: if a baseline supports GPU computation, it was run on the same GPU as GALA; otherwise, it was executed on the same CPU. Details of the operating system and device configuration are provided in  Supplementary Section S2.3 . Across multiple benchmarks, GALA demonstrated superior computational efficiency, achieving both faster runtime and substantially lower memory usage compared with existing methods. It consistently outperformed other nonlinear methods, being substantially faster than GPSA and ST-GEARS (averaging 135.22 s compared with 245.61 and 154.69 s, respectively, on slices 2 and 3 of Sample C), while also maintaining a minimal memory footprint. While specialized rigid methods like PASTE, STAligner, and SLAT were faster (all under 30 s), they required substantially more memory and yielded inferior accuracy. Furthermore, GALA also outperformed STalign, its primary competitor built on the same LDDMM core, across multiple datasets. For example, on the human breast cancer dataset, GALA achieved an average runtime of 74.16 s with minimal memory usage, compared with STalign’s 512.06 s and substantially higher memory consumption, due to GALA’s streamlined optimization and reduced parameters (see Section Alignment objective and optimization).  GALA also excelled at scale where many methods failed due to excessive memory demands (e.g. 500 GB, MERFISH mouse liver data); it successfully aligned datasets of hundreds of thousands of cells in under a minute, far outpacing SLAT’s lengthy cell-matching phase. This efficiency extended to multimodal and mismatched-resolution scenarios, solidifying GALA’s advantage for rapid, low memory usage, high-fidelity alignment of large-scale ST data. The details of comparison of computational efficiency with baseline methods are provided at  Supplementary Table S4 .     Discussion and Conclusion  In this study, we introduced GALA, a unified, landmark-free spatial alignment framework capable of addressing a wide range of challenges in ST alignment. A central strength of GALA lies in its multimodal rasterization strategy, which converts diverse transcriptomic and histological data into co-registered raster tensors. This standardized representation harmonizes heterogeneous resolutions, modalities, and sequencing platforms, and naturally scales from spot-level to dense single-cell data, enabling the aggregation of millions of cells onto a user-defined grid where each pixel encodes local features. By design, GALA jointly leverages transcriptomic and histological information with tunable weights, enhancing both alignment accuracy and interpretability. Its coarse-to-fine optimization couples a GA transformation, which identifies overlapping regions for initialization, with an EM-like LDDMM refinement capable of large-scale deformations. The EM-style probabilistic matching focuses alignment on confidently corresponding regions while downweighting background or artefacts, making the coupled strategy robust across resolutions, modalities, and partial tissue overlaps. Furthermore, the invertibility of the diffeomorphic transformation ensures directionally consistent alignment. In within-resolution tasks, source-to-target and target-to-source alignments yield highly similar performance ( Supplementary Section S2.2.1, Fig. S8 ). For cross-resolution or cross-modality alignment, the same property allows the high-resolution modality to be stably aligned to a lower-resolution reference, while the inverse transformation naturally provides the corresponding reverse mapping ( Supplementary Fig. S16 ).  Compared with existing approaches ( Table 1 ), GALA offers broader applicability and improved robustness. Spot-level methods such as PASTE and STAligner emphasize rigid alignment, whereas STalign and GPSA provide non-rigid deformations but with limited modality support or scalability. SLAT relies on one-to-one graph matching, which restricts its flexibility in heterogeneous tissue contexts. Coarse-to-fine frameworks such as ST-GEARS are specialized for particular modalities or task types, and most baselines, except for PASTE2, cannot handle partial tissue overlaps. In contrast, GALA uniquely integrates rigid and non-rigid deformations within a coupled framework and supports spot-to-spot, cell-to-cell, cell-to-spot, and transcriptomic-to-histology alignment across both full and partial tissue overlaps. While STalign also employs LDDMM, it cannot leverage gene expression or H&E image data, does not support spot-to-spot or direct cell-to-spot alignment, and relies on manually defined landmarks. Despite its strengths, several limitations of GALA should be considered. Multimodal fusion of transcriptomic and histological data does not always improve alignment, reflecting both methodological constraints and the inherent biological reality that molecular and morphological states are not perfectly concordant [ 48 ]. Morphologically similar cells may exhibit distinct molecular profiles, and sharp molecular boundaries may lack histological counterparts [ 47 ]. Such discordances can introduce noise, highlighting the need for adaptive, biologically informed fusion strategies that weight each modality based on local context [ 3 ]. Furthermore, GALA focuses on geometric spatial alignment and does not explicitly correct gene expression batch effects. In datasets with substantial donor variability or platform differences, additional downstream integration methods may be required after alignment to harmonize molecular signals. Finally, as with all LDDMM-based frameworks, GALA assumes smooth, diffeomorphic deformations. Extremely irregular, discontinuous, or topology-disrupting distortions may violate this assumption and thus fall outside the model’s representational capacity, leading to alignment failure ( Supplementary Section S2.2.2 ).  Nonetheless, by providing accurate and flexible spatial alignment, GALA establishes a critical foundation for downstream applications, including cross-sample atlas construction, consistent cell-type mapping, and trajectory inference. For example, GALA ensures spatial correspondence across samples, while network-based models (e.g. Perturb-STNet [ 17 ]) capture cell–cell interactions and perturbation effects within the aligned coordinate system, enabling integrative analyses that combine geometric alignment with functional modelling. Beyond transcriptomics, GALA is readily extendable to other spatially resolved omics modalities, such as spatial proteomics or metabolomics [ 49 ,  50 ]. By aggregating molecular measurements onto a common spatial grid through rasterization, multi-omics data can be aligned within a unified framework. These representations may further be embedded into shared latent spaces using representation learning approaches, facilitating cross-modality comparison of spatial patterns while preserving modality-specific variation. Future work will explore joint multimodal alignment while addressing cross-modality consistency and heterogeneous noise. Taken together, integrating precise spatial alignment with downstream biological modelling represents a promising direction. We anticipate that GALA will serve as a versatile component within broader spatial omics pipelines, potentially coupled with modules for spatially informed gene expression modelling, or used to infer conserved spatial programmes across individuals, conditions, and technologies.    Key points    GALA (Genetic Algorithm–guided Large Deformation Alignment) targets spatial alignment across heterogeneous spatial transcriptomics (ST) datasets, supporting practical application scenarios including cross-platform and cross-resolution alignment, cross-modality integration, and partial tissue alignment.    GALA implements a fully automated, landmark-free alignment framework that jointly models both global affine transformation and local diffeomorphic deformation within a unified multimodal representation.    GALA demonstrates robust and accurate alignment across diverse alignment scenarios encountered in real-world ST applications, while scaling to large tissue sections and facilitating downstream integrative analyses. evidence_text:
Unraveling lncRNA diversity at a single cell resolution and in a spatial context across different cancer types. Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) participate in gene regulation underlying development and disease. Overcoming inherent limitations of bulk sequencing lncRNA analysis, we leveraged single-cell and spatial transcriptomics (ST) data to analyze 219,442 potential lncRNAs identified by the TAR-scRNA-seq pipeline across 13 cancer types. The lncRNA functions were assessed by identifying their cell-type specificity and spatial distributions across different tissue regions. Comparing with five existing databases, we confirmed shared lncRNAs and found 94,795 unannotated lncRNAs. The identified lncRNAs were experimentally validated across seven cancer types using three single-cell-resolution ST platforms and two long-read ST sequencing methods, encompassing both targeted and untargeted approaches. Genome-wide colocalization of lncRNAs with regulatory features, disease variants and pairwise spatial autocorrelation with protein-coding genes suggest potential functional roles. We built a free, fast and user-friendly database 'SPanC-Lnc' on AWS cloud. SPanC-Lnc will enable discovery of potentially functional lncRNAs specific for cell populations within heterogeneous tissues, providing new biological insights. Main  Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) constitute the majority of the permissively transcribed genome. Despite this, the majority of our knowledge about transcriptional events is limited to the 1–2% of the genome that encodes proteins  1  . With advancements in high-throughput technologies, it has become increasingly apparent that lncRNAs are of functional relevance, contributing to diseases like cancer where they are often misregulated  2  .  The lncRNAs serve as a valuable class of molecular targets for disease identification; however, their detection has been constrained by factors such as their low abundance, cell-type-specific expression patterns and the reliance of existing computational tools on previous annotations  3  . Previous studies on lncRNAs have predominantly relied on bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data, which unfortunately results in the loss of cell-type information and tissue spatial context, both of which are essential for understanding transcriptional regulation in developmental and diseased states. The spatial information provides valuable insights into a transcript’s location within a tissue, its neighboring cells, colocalizing transcripts or proteins and their interacting partners, thereby enhancing our comprehension of biological processes.  Advanced technologies such as single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics (ST) sequence transcripts at the single-cell level while preserving spatial information. Up to 40% of lncRNAs are polyadenylated and an additional 40% of them are bimorphic  4  . Thus, using a polyA-capture protocol, such as 10x Visium, these transcripts can be analyzed. Recent studies using scRNA-seq for breast cancer samples  5 , 6   evaluated known (annotated) lncRNAs at a single-cell level. Other studies claiming to have analyzed the ‘spatial transcriptome’ of lncRNAs have typically examined lncRNA expression across different bulk tissues, rather than capturing the nuanced expression patterns of lncRNAs within a tissue section  7 , 8  . These studies did not explore novel unannotated lncRNAs. Several methods for novel transcript identification have been established for bulk sequencing data  9 , 10  . Applying these methods to ST and scRNA-seq data would not only facilitate the expansion of annotations but also unveil additional layers of information regarding lncRNAs, including cell-type specificity and spatial context to reveal physical manifestation of their crosstalk with protein-coding genes. Although these technologies have not yet addressed the identification of non-polyadenylated lncRNAs or the entire spectrum of rare lncRNAs, creating a repository of potential lncRNAs detected through cutting-edge ST technologies would establish a robust foundation for biological discovery.  In this study, we combined large datasets from the spatially resolved RNA sequencing by 10x Visium and single-cell resolution scRNA-seq by 10x Chromium to discover lncRNAs in tissues from 13 different cancer types, along with cross-validation on samples from the more recent technologies like STOmics, Takara Bio Seeker and Xenium in situ. We demonstrated new types of analyses to identify potential functions of lncRNAs. While previous pan-cancer studies have examined clinically relevant lncRNAs  11 – 13  , this study constitutes a large-scale, spatially resolved investigation of uncharacterized or new potential lncRNAs, integrating cell-type-specific information to advance our understanding of their roles in cancer (Supplementary Table  1 ). The annotations and lncRNA expression data of each tissue are accessible through the interactive website ‘SPanC-Lnc’: Spatial and Single Cell Pan-Cancer Atlas of lncRNAs at  https://spanclnc.click/ . Researchers and clinicians can leverage this resource to gain deeper insights into the roles of lncRNAs in cancer biology.    Results   Identification of potential lncRNAs in spatial and single-cell datasets  Samples from 28 previously published in-house ST and 24 scRNA-seq samples across 13 cancer types were analyzed for potential novel lncRNAs (Fig.  1a ) using the TAR-scRNA-seq pipeline  10  . The cumulative expression of all unannotated transcriptionally active regions (uTARs) detected in each sample was projected on the corresponding tissues and compared to that of the cumulative coding gene expression. Three representative examples for different cancer types are displayed in Fig.  1b . uTAR and coding gene expression for the remaining samples are also shown in Supplementary Figs.  1  and  2 , respectively. The expression of several previously identified cancer-specific lncRNAs was also visualized (Supplementary Fig.  3 ). It is worth noting that while lncRNAs like  MALAT1  and  NORAD  were abundantly expressed across the tissue sections in various samples (Supplementary Fig.  3a ), others displayed a certain degree of tissue specificity. For instance, both  PICSAR  and  LINC00520 , known to be squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)-specific  14  , were markedly more expressed in cutaneous SCC and head and neck (H&N) oropharyngeal SCC (OPSCC) compared to the other cancer types. In contrast, while  PICSAR  and  LINC00520  were either absent or expressed at lower levels in breast and colorectal cancer (CRC),  TINCR  (known to play oncogenic roles in breast cancer  15 , 16  ) was highly expressed in breast cancer samples (Supplementary Fig.  3b ).  TINCR  is also known to be oncogenic in OPSCC and tumor suppressing in SCC and highly expressed in our representative samples. Similarly,  KCNQ1OT1  (commonly implicated in CRC prognosis  17 , 18  ) showed higher expression in the CRC sample compared to other lncRNAs expressed in this sample. Numbers highlighted in red indicate the number of cuTARs detected for each cancer type, followed by the number of samples analyzed within square brackets.  b , uTAR counts overlaid on the tissue for representative samples as compared to the protein-coding gene counts.  c , Breakdown of known and novel uTARs identified per cancer sample. Source data                        The samples used and the number of uTARs identified are summarized in Fig.  1c , with the numbers varying, depending on the cancer type and coverage. For example, a higher number of uTARs were found in breast cancer samples (~45,000–60,000) and one kidney cancer sample (namely KidA) (~45,000), whereas 4,000–25,000 were detected in other samples. Overall, more uTARs were detected with scRNA-seq compared to ST, as scRNA-seq generally captures a higher number of cells. In most samples, approximately 40–60% of the identified uTARs overlapped with lncRNAs cataloged in lncRNA public databases such as FANTOM, LncBook, LNCipedia and NONCODE (Fig.  1c ). Moreover, while our initial analyses used GENCODE v.43 to filter out annotated transcripts, the recent v.47 release has expanded lncRNA annotations  19  . To account for this update, we retained uTARs that overlap lncRNA or noncoding pseudogene annotations in v.47 but were unannotated in v.43. Many of these had been identified by our method, demonstrating transcripts that we identified as unannotated lncRNAs in v.43 are now recognized as lncRNAs in GENCODE v.47. The remaining transcripts are likely novel discoveries not yet reported by other databases and merit further investigation (Fig.  1c ).  The relative uTAR:gene counts for each tissue at Visium spot-level resolution was calculated as the total number of uTARs divided by the total number of genes detected per spot (Fig.  1d ). A higher value indicates a higher number of total uTARs detected per Visium spot with respect to the number of coding genes, as in the melanoma samples (Fig.  1d ); however, this could be due to the lower sample quality (<200 median genes per spot). As the uTARs analyzed in this study span various cancer types and tissues, we merged overlapping uTARs across multiple samples into a single uTAR. These were designated as cancer-associated uTARs (cuTARs) (Supplementary Fig.  4 ) and assigned unique numerical identifiers in our SPanC-Lnc database. The terms uTAR, cuTAR and lncRNA are used interchangeably throughout the paper. A total of 47 cuTARs were expressed on a pan-cancer level (expressed in at least one sample per cancer type in the study) and 1,278 in at least ten cancer types, whereas most of the others exhibited specificity to particular cancer types (Extended Data Fig.  1a,b ). The consistency of detection across different sequencing platforms (ST, 3’ and 5’ scRNA-seq) for melanoma samples was also analyzed. About 1,574 cuTARs were detected in melanoma samples across all the three different platforms (Extended Data Fig.  1c ). Following these findings, we further investigated some of these potential disease-associated candidates in specific cancer types.    Characterization of cuTAR transcripts  To further define cuTAR structure, we overlapped cuTAR coordinates with transcription start site (TSS) annotations from FANTOM, poly-A sites (PAS) and splice sites (Fig.  1e ). They were classified as cuTARs with (1) complete evidence (overlapping with a TSS at the 5′ end and a PAS at the 3′ end within a 1.5-kb window upstream and downstream, respectively); (2) partial evidence comprising of first exons (TSS at the 5′ end and a donor site junction at the 3′ end), internal exons (acceptor site at the 5′ end and a donor site at the 3′ end) and last exons (acceptor site at the 5′ end and PAS at the 3’ end); and (3) incomplete evidence if it overlapped with either TSS or PAS (Fig.  1e ). Overall, 9.07% cuTARs had complete evidence (Fig.  1e ) and 24.9% cuTARs had PAS, last and internal exon evidence, potentially indicating that these transcripts have at least two exons. Overall, 27% cuTARs had only PAS evidence, which is expected as most cuTARs were biased to the 3′ end. To collect further evidence, the cuTARs were overlapped with the new lncRNA annotations from GENCODE v.47 since the release v.43 (Fig.  1e ). Overlapping cuTARs with human permissive enhancers from FANTOM, we found that 3.32% were enhancer-derived lncRNAs (e-lncRNAs) with an enhancer overlap at the 5′ end and 7.29% with an enhancer spanning anywhere along the cuTAR sequence. Additionally, to ensure cuTARs are independent and not potential read-throughs of nearby genes, we labeled those located within 10 kb downstream of coding genes as ‘less confident’ (12.5% of cuTARs).  The sequences were analyzed using CPAT and RNAsamba for coding potential. The CPAT algorithm results are affected by the length of the transcript. RNAsamba is an alternative coding potential calculator that works well on partial-length sequences  20  . RNAsamba identified 97% of all cuTARs to be noncoding. While CPAT filtered out many cuTARs, RNAsamba retained most of them and inferred the coding potential. Overall, 76.6% of cuTARs were predicted to be noncoding using both the tools and 98.3% of the total cuTARs lacked coding potential (Fig.  1f ). The lncRNAs with a coding potential might indicate their role in encoding functional micropeptides, as opposed to necessarily being protein-coding transcripts  21 , 22  . As the cuTARs represent estimated transcript boundaries using data captured from either the 3′ or 5′ ends, the calculated coding potentials may be less accurate than those obtained using the full-length sequence, but they can still provide a meaningful reflection of their coding potential. Moreover, 94.75% of them were at least 200 bp, suggesting that the majority of cuTARs were most likely to be ‘long’ ncRNAs  23  .  Additionally, we predict splice sites utilizing AlphaGenome  24  . To evaluate AlphaGenome predictions, we visualized the  BIRC5  gene (Extended Data Fig.  2a ) and compared the predicted splice sites with the RefSeq exon annotations for the cuTARs that have been annotated in GENCODE v.47 but were unannotated as of v.43 (Extended Data Fig.  2b ). In most cases, predicted splice site peaks were consistent with the annotated exon–intron junctions. With this serving as a performance reference, we were able to predict and suggest potential splice sites in the unannotated and uncharacterized cuTARs (Fig.  1g ).  Conservation and minimum free energy (MFE) are useful metrics for assessing sequence functionality and were calculated for the H&N sample C (HNC). Most top cuTAR candidates had lower conservation than  GAPDH  or the lncRNA  HOTAIR . They also had a stable secondary structure (Supplementary Fig.  5a ).  The genetic-level regulation of the cuTARs through enrichment of eQTL and GWAS SNPs are elaborated in Supplementary Note  1  (Supplementary Figs.  5b  and  6–8 ).    Identification of lncRNAs enriched in cancer tissue regions  Next, we asked whether the cuTAR expression was restricted specifically to the tumor area within the biopsies. Given that lncRNAs can be present in both healthy and tumor tissues, tumor specificity was defined by enrichment within cancerous regions annotated by a pathologist and where histological annotation was unavailable (for example, CP), inferred from tumor-associated gene expression patterns (Fig.  2a ). Top cuTAR candidates for each cancer type were shortlisted based on their detection across various datasets and higher expression in the annotated cancerous regions. The percentage of spots in the cancerous versus normal regions expressing the selected cuTARs in the H&N OPSCC samples were calculated (Fig.  2b ). Source data                        The expression of these top cuTAR candidates was detected across many cancer types from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)  25   bulk RNA-seq samples. Some cuTARs showed higher expression in the seven TCGA OPSCC samples used, consistent with the observation that all these candidates were tumor-specific in the H&N ST data (Fig.  2b ). Among the cuTARs differentially expressed across these two annotated regions (Supplementary Fig.  9 ), visual examination of gene expression overlaid on the tissues reveal some cuTARs with higher expression in the tumor regions (Fig.  2a,c ). Not only cancer region specificity, but also subclone specificity was observed. The tumor subclones were identified based on inferred copy-number variation using CopyKAT  26   (Extended Data Fig.  3 ).    Confirmation of lncRNA detection using spatial long-read sequencing  Since the 10x Visium protocol captures only the 3′ ends of fragmented transcripts, the actual transcripts are likely longer than the detected cuTAR boundaries. To increase confidence in transcript identification, we applied long-read sequencing using Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) and PacBio MAS-Seq (Pacific Biosciences) to unfragmented cDNA from 10x Visium libraries. Although these libraries remain 3′ biased, long-read sequencing yields longer fragments, allowing more confident mapping of cuTAR signals than using Visium short read data. We found the signals detected to be consistent across different technologies, suggesting that these cuTARs were likely to be genuine signals rather than artifacts from the TAR-scRNA-seq pipeline.  10x Visium unfragmented cDNA libraries from the HNC (OPSCC), SCC and basal cell carcinoma (BCC) samples were used for the ONT experiment. As a representative example, from HNC, we obtained ~16 million ONT reads, with 3,888 spatial barcodes identified by the scNanoGPS pipeline  27  , allowing us to map to 1,028 Visium spots across the tissue. We successfully recovered ~83.6% reads that were complete (with spatial barcode, unique molecular identifiers (UMIs), 3′ adaptors and poly-A/T tails), identifying approximately 985 cuTARs (Supplementary Table  2 ), 960 of which were present in at least three spots overlapping the tissue. This accounts for 31.7% of those detected using 10x Visium, thus validating the detection of uTAR expression from the short-read data. Similar spatial patterns were observed (Fig.  2d ), with up to 38% of spots showing expression in both the technologies and up to 86% for coding genes (Supplementary Note  2  and Supplementary Fig.  10 ). Notably, when we applied the TAR-scRNA-seq pipeline directly to the Nanopore BAM files, we identified 32 novel uTARs not detected with the short-read data. In addition, we confirmed signals from the transcriptionally active region (TAR) annotations generated using the 10x Visium data, where 857 ONT uTARs (807 cuTARs) were also detected in the HNC Visium sample. Overall, 92 additional cuTARs detected with ONT were present in our entire database but not in the corresponding Visium sample. To evaluate the results, the consistency of expression patterns for coding genes were also verified (Supplementary Fig.  10 ). There was a substantial overlap of expressing spots across both the platforms for some cuTARs (Extended Data Fig.  4a ). The same analysis was performed for cutaneous SCC and BCC using ONT (Extended Data Fig.  4b,c ).  For the PacBio MAS-Seq long read sequencing run with complementary DNA of CRC samples from the 10x Visium experiment, we generated approximately 1 million HiFi reads. By aligning the reads and tagging them with spatial barcode information, we found up to 1,500 lncRNAs per sample, which accounted for up to ~20% of those detected with 10x Visium (Extended Data Fig.  4d ), thereby also confirming the findings of the 10x Visium Illumina data. We then examined specific cuTARs and found that up to 30% of the spots showed statistically significant consistency in expression for the same set of spots across both the platforms for two CRC-specific cuTARs (Fig.  2d  and Extended Data Fig.  4b,c ) (for example, cuTAR86784, 19%;  P  = 0.011; cuTAR114310, 29%;  P   =  0.014). Overall, we found the PacBio sequencing mapping efficiency was better than that of ONT considering the number of uniquely mapping cuTARs identified for the number of reads captured and processed. More quality control (QC) statistics for long-read spatial sequencing are described in Supplementary Tables  2  and  3 .    Takara Bio Seeker and STOmics spatial data confirmed cuTARs at single-cell resolution  The cuTAR detection at single cell resolution was analyzed with Takara Bio Seeker for one breast cancer and one melanoma sample. We observed consistent expression patterns of coding genes generated using the Takara Bio Seeker pipeline (Extended Data Fig.  5a ) and the TAR-scRNA-seq pipeline (Extended Data Fig.  5a ) in the breast cancer sample. Some previously identified breast-cancer-specific cuTARs were also visualized (Extended Data Fig.  5b ). Similarly, annotated genes and melanoma-specific cuTARs were visualized on the melanoma sample (Extended Data Fig.  5c,d ). Overall, 31.4% of the cuTARs identified from Visium and scRNA-seq breast cancer data were also detected in the Seeker breast cancer sample, while 47.56% of those from melanoma data overlapped with the Seeker melanoma sample.  Additionally, we performed STOmics OMNI sequencing for melanoma and CRC samples. cuTAR counts were generated using the SAW pipeline with Visium and scRNA-seq identified cuTAR coordinates as a custom GTF input. 116,862 (52.7%) cuTARs were detected in at least three cells of the STOmics data (Fig.  2e ). Total cuTAR counts across the tissues is shown in Supplementary Fig.  11a . Higher expression of some melanoma-specific cuTARs identified using scRNA-seq data was observed in the melanoma sample compared to the CRC samples (Supplementary Fig.  11b ). To enable a more unbiased discovery of cuTARs that may be non-polyadenylated, we next applied the TAR-scRNA-seq pipeline directly to the aligned STOmics BAM files at the bulk level. This strategy allowed for de novo identification of uTARs with transcript boundaries independent of Visium, complementing our earlier analysis where transcript counts were restricted to Visium-defined transcripts. The spatial expression patterns of exemplar breast- and melanoma-specific cuTARs are visualized on the Takara Bio Seeker and STOmics datasets (Fig.  2f ).    Experimental detection of lncRNA using quantitative reverse transcription PCR  We further experimentally validated and quantified seven cuTARs by qRT–PCR. With specific primers targeting each of the selected cuTARs (Supplementary Table  4 ), we found cuTARs in the H&N samples (HNC and HNB), SCC, BCC and CRC samples. All the lncRNAs were detected, except cuTAR121087, which showed a low PCR signal, although high expression was detected with Visium for the HNC sample and other samples (Supplementary Figs.  12  and  13 ). Further results are discussed in Supplementary Note  3 .    Inferring potential functions by spatial coexpression analysis of lncRNAs with cancer-associated genes  Transcripts that are expressed together tend to function together. For data-driven prediction of functional cuTARs, we used bivariate Moran’s index ( I ) to identify coexpression patterns between spatially variable cuTARs (Supplementary Fig.  14a ) and cancer-hallmark genes, suggesting possible co-regulation gene networks between uncharacterized cuTARs and known cancer-associated genes. Figure  3a  shows four top cuTARs with more than 50 high–high (HH) spots showing coexpression with a greater number of cancer-relevant genes compared to the other cuTARs in the H&N sample C (HNC). Some cuTARs were coexpressed with many genes involved in cancer associated pathways, especially the P53 pathway and G2M checkpoint (Fig.  3a ), whereas in a kidney cancer sample (KidD), high coexpression was observed with genes involved in epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) and the P53 pathway (Supplementary Fig.  14b ). These cuTARs, although detected in healthy kidney tissue, have a significantly lower expression compared to other kidney cancer samples (Supplementary Fig.  14c ). Examples of spatially coexpressed cuTARs and coding genes in the H&N sample are shown in Fig.  3b . For example, cuTAR213507 (chr4:182814299–182820899 (+)) was coexpressed with the messenger RNA of  FGFR3 , a gene upregulated in H&N cancers, also on chromosome 4 (chr4:1793293–1808867 (+)). A total of 24 other cancer-relevant genes are located on the same chromosome with this top spatially autocorrelated cuTAR, suggesting strong evidence for a cancer-associated cuTAR. Moreover, this cuTAR is downstream to a recently annotated lncRNA ENSG00000309834 and the gene  TENM3 .  TENM3  is upregulated in several cancers compared to healthy tissues, particularly in H&N SCCs, pancreatic adenocarcinoma, thymoma and neuroblastoma  28  . It also serves as an integration site for the human papilloma virus (HPV), causing cervical and a large proportion of oropharyngeal cancers  29   and also harbors a genome-wide association study (GWAS) single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)  rs1516535 , an intron variant associated with HPV infection in oropharyngeal cancers. It is worth mentioning that the OPSCC samples utilized in this study were HPV-16 +  (ref.   30  ). Fusions of  TENM3  gene have been reported to induce cell proliferation  31  . Source data                        Using coexpression network analyses with hdWGCNA, we identified that one of the top candidates cuTAR170206 (LncBook  HSALNG0133452 ) formed part of a coexpression module with genes enriched for various cancer hallmarks. Additionally, it was found to be highly coexpressed with  NDRG1  (Fig.  3c ), which is known to be downregulated in metastatic OPSCC tumors  32  . In this particular case,  NDRG1  was seen to be expressed only in the periphery and not in the core of the tumor (Fig.  3c ). This gene has been shown to have pleiotropic functions, acting as tumor promoters in some cancers, while playing a tumor suppressor role in others  33  . This modulation in function could potentially be attributed to its association with interacting lncRNAs.    Inferring functions by machine-learning prediction of interaction with RBPs and colocalization  The lncRNAs interact with RNA binding proteins (RBPs) to regulate mRNA and protein localization and functions  34  . Several machine-learning models that have been trained on known lncRNA–RBP interactions can help predict new interactions. We applied HLPI-Ensemble  35   to predict the interaction of the shortlisted cuTARs with RBPs. A noteworthy association for cuTAR215705 was observed in the ST breast cancer sample (BreastA) (Fig.  3d ). cuTAR215705 was predicted to interact with the RBPs, HuR (ELAVL1) and TARDBP (TDP-43). Moreover, these were part of the same coexpression module identified through hdWGCNA, which is enriched for TGF-β negative regulation and positive regulation of protein localization (Supplementary Fig.  14d ). Additionally, it shares this module with the gene  BIRC5 , which has recently been reported to interact with ELAVL1. Previous reports indicate that recombinant ELAVL1 is linked to the upregulation of  BIRC5  expression, whereas its silencing correlates with the downregulation of both  BIRC5  mRNA and protein, accompanied by increased apoptosis. Survival analyses from a previous study demonstrated that increased  TTP  ( ZFP36 ) and low  BIRC5  expression predicted an overall better prognosis compared to dysregulated  TTP  and high  BIRC5  (ref.   36  ). cuTAR215705 colocalized with  BIRC5  and  ELAVL1  in the tumor cells (Fig.  3e ). The colocalization was significant in the tumor region of the tissue and the absence or reduced expression of both the cuTAR and the two aforementioned genes ( BIRC5  and  ELAVL1 ) was observed in other cell types (Supplementary Fig.  14e ).    Examples of cell-type-specific lncRNAs (cuTARs) associated with response to cancer therapy   Case study 1: cell-type-specific lncRNAs in acral and cutaneous melanoma and their associations with response to anti-PD-1 immunotherapy  To demonstrate a deeper analysis to explore possible functions of the cuTARs in this atlas, a public scRNA-seq acral and cutaneous melanoma dataset was analyzed to identify cell-type-specific lncRNAs (cuTARs) and to analyze their response to anti-PD-1 immunotherapy (Supplementary Fig.  15 ). The lncRNAs differentially expressed in each cell-type (Supplementary Fig.  16a,b ) were identified with edgeR  37   (Fig.  4a ) and expression of a subset were visualized on Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) (Fig.  4b ). The cuTARs upregulated in the tumor cells show coexpression with respective proximal protein-coding genes associated with melanoma (Fig.  4c ). For example, we observed the co-upregulation of cuTARs with pigmentation genes  PMEL  (cuTAR67350 LncBook HSALNG0094046) and  MLANA  (cuTAR293520)  38  . Additionally, cuTAR280980 exhibited coexpression with  ESRP1 , encoding a master splicing regulator in EMT  39  , an annotated lncRNA,  LINC00589  (also known as  TSLNC8 ), implicated in diverse roles across different cancer types  40  , and with  ANXA1 , known to be upregulated in invasive melanomas  41  . This suggests that these cuTARs could be part of regulatory modules influencing tumor progression. Validation of lncRNA detection, cancer specificity and coexpression patterns with Xenium customized panel  We performed Xenium in situ hybridization to independently assess findings from Visium and scRNA-seq, enabling us to visualize targets at a cellular level. We designed a custom Xenium panel comprising 76 cuTARs (Supplementary Table  5 ). Overall, all the cuTARs were found to be expressed, substantially higher than the signals from gDNA negative control probes (Extended Data Fig.  8a ). Differential expression analysis confirmed the cancer-type specificity of cuTARs, previously observed with scRNA-seq and Visium (Fig.  6a ). The cuTARs were visualized at a single-cell resolution and were seen to be specific to the predicted tumor cells (red polygons) across different cancer types (Fig.  6b ). The coexpression patterns with coding genes shown in Fig.  3e  were also confirmed. Two particular cuTARs specific to breast cancer samples were analyzed for their coexpression and prognostic value, cuTAR215705 and cuTAR32998 (GENCODE v.47  LOC107984223 ). These were found to be coexpressed with  BIRC5  and associated RBPs (Fig.  3e ). The coexpression and localization of one of the cuTARs, cuTAR215705 with  ELAVL1  and  BIRC5  at a subcellular level in one of the breast cancer samples is shown Extended Data Fig.  8b–d ; however, these two cuTARs often were not coexpressed. The exact  P  value displayed in the plot was computed using a two-sided log-rank (Mantel–Cox) test implemented via the survdiff() function from the survival R package for the cuTARs, and obtained from cBioPortal for  BIRC5 .   Source data                        The differences in expression patterns were replicated in samples across 10x Visium, Xenium, Takara Bio Seeker and 10x Chromium scRNA-seq (Fig.  6c ). Moreover, in the TCGA breast cancer cohort 246 patients), cuTAR215705 was associated with poor survival, whereas cuTAR32998 correlated with better survival. Notably, these cuTARs stratified patients more efficiently than the coding gene  BIRC5  (Fig.  6d ).    A spatial and single cell pan-cancer atlas of lncRNAs  The findings of this study have been made publicly available through our database ‘ SPanC-Lnc ’ on AWS cloud (Extended Data Fig.  9 ). A total of 219,442 cuTARs across 13 broad cancer types were identified using scRNA-seq and 10x Visium ST, further validated using five ST platforms. This resource allows users to interactively query lncRNA/cuTAR annotations in a user-friendly UCSC-style genome browser, providing visualizations for cross-cancer expression comparisons, cell-type specificity via UMAP overlays and spatial localization within tumor sections. Users can also retrieve splice junction predictions and associated metadata using the table browser. The metadata includes information about cancer/cell-type specificity, overlap with public lncRNA databases, structural characterization and cross-platform validations. SPanC-Lnc is a large pan-cancer resource of known and new lncRNAs with single cell and spatial contexts. Resources like FANTOM-CAT, LncBook and NONCODE provide lncRNA annotations mostly from bulk RNA-seq data of cell lines and tissues (Supplementary Table  1 ). SPanC-Lnc has lncRNAs with cell type and spatial resolution, lacking from bulk RNA-seq. Recent studies utilizing scRNA-seq and ST data have explored the expression of annotated lncRNAs  5 , 6 , 44 , 45  ; however, information on a pan-cancer scale for potential novel lncRNAs is not available. SPanC-Lnc not only provides annotations and transcript characterization, but also expression comparisons across different cancer types and cell-types and analyzes their potential putative functions. The resource is structured to accommodate incorporation of additional datasets and analytical refinements, and transcript annotations may be further refined as new data become available or as structural and functional validations provide additional evidence. The modular design and documented workflows facilitate transparency, reproducibility and potential future extensions of the atlas.     Discussion  This study utilized advanced transcriptomics technologies for uncovering a diverse repertoire of previously unannotated and/or uncharacterized lncRNAs in cancer. Through integrative analysis across multiple cancer types, we identified lncRNAs exhibiting dynamic expression patterns and tumor-specific spatial distributions, suggesting their potential roles as major regulators in tumorigenesis and cancer progression.  At a structural level, lncRNAs could be derived from enhancers, promoters, pseudogenes or transposons. The lncRNAs derived from the transcription of active enhancers (e-lncRNAs) are known to participate in many cancer-associated biological processes like angiogenesis, proliferation, invasion and metastasis  46 – 49  . At the genetic level, disease-associated GWAS SNPs or eQTLs could regulate nearby protein-coding genes through altering the levels of colocalizing lncRNAs  50  . Spatial autocorrelation with coding genes involved in several cancer-related pathways revealed coexpression of these novel lncRNAs in pathways associated with cell cycle, cellular proliferation, immune response, angiogenesis, hypoxia and metastasis, highlighting their putative involvement in critical biological processes underlying cancer development.  In our study, reads within a 500-bp window were merged and annotated as a single uTAR. While this heuristic simplifies annotation, it introduces potential limitations. For example, a long cuTAR (defined from overlapping uTARs across samples) may represent merged signals from independent transcripts, or adjacent cuTARs may be conflated into a single transcript. This was particularly evident in the higher-resolution STOmics/Takara Bio dataset, where longer transcript boundaries led to the merging of multiple Visium-derived cuTARs into a single STOmics cuTAR. Notably, cuTAR discovery and characterization were based primarily on Visium and scRNA-seq data, where transcript boundaries are shorter and more conservative, reducing the risk of over-merging during novel lncRNA identification. STOmics/Takara Bio data were used for validation rather than discovery, and in many cases the extended boundaries reinforced the presence of a single transcript by extending its annotated range. We prioritized expression specificity, reproducibility and biological association (for example, cancer state, treatment response and cell type) rather than precise transcript boundaries. Consequently, the biological signal and specificity of these cuTARs remain robust despite minor annotation discrepancies. This atlas provides a biologically relevant set of cancer-specific, cell-type-specific and treatment-responsive lncRNAs that already serves as a foundation for biological discovery and can be further refined as transcript annotations improve.  While poly-adenylated lncRNAs were the main focus of this study, other classes of ncRNAs like circular RNAs (circRNAs)  51 , 52  , pre-miRNAs/miRNAs  53  , piRNAs  54 , 55   and non-polyadenylated lncRNAs  56   are also aberrantly expressed in cancers and gene regulation. The identification of these lncRNAs in addition to the new lncRNA panel put forth in this study would serve as a valuable resource for future investigations. Notably, we also added STOmics (random hexamer capture) data to complement polyA-capture methods. We detected 93,255 new uTARs and 105,701 uTARs overlapping with 41,573 entries in databases like LncBook, LNCipedia and NONCODE. Of these, 63,584 uTARs overlap with 32,202 lncRNAs on the same strand. This suggests that some of these uTARs may be non-polyadenylated lncRNAs, making them worthwhile candidates for further investigation in future studies.  A large number of lncRNAs identified from scRNA-seq and ST data can be assigned as highly expressed markers specific to subpopulations of cells, including rare cells. SPanC-Lnc constitutes a scalable resource for investigating fundamental aspects of lncRNA biology, offering new approaches to identifying new lncRNAs and inferring their functions at single-cell and spatial resolution. By systematically comparing lncRNA expression across diverse cellular subpopulations, the discovery framework enables interrogation of cell-type specificity, transcriptional heterogeneity and context-dependent expression patterns that are not accessible through bulk RNA-seq. The integration of spatial information further allows examination of how lncRNA expression varies across tissue architecture, such as tumor cores, immune-rich regions and invasive margins. This spatially resolved view provides an opportunity to study microenvironment-associated transcriptional programs and to generate testable hypotheses about lncRNA regulation in situ, for example through the colocalization and co-regulation of lncRNA with coding genes and pathways. Notably, SPanC-Lnc establishes a standardized computational strategy for integrating single-cell and spatial datasets to annotate, prioritize and visualize lncRNAs across different technology platforms and cancer types. As such, it provides a reference database that can be extended to include additional datasets for more tissues, disease states and emerging single-cell and ST technologies. By enabling systematic exploration of the noncoding transcriptome at a cellular resolution, this resource facilitates mechanistic studies aimed at defining the regulatory principles governing lncRNA expression and functions.    Methods   Primary datasets   Spatial transcriptomics datasets across different cancers  Previously published in-house datasets from fresh frozen tissues of different cancer types (kidney  57  , SCC, BCC  58  , H&N OPSCC  30  , medulloblastoma  42  , CRC  59   and breast cancers  60  ) and clinical formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) biopsies of melanoma  61   were used in this study (10x Visium poly-A capture). One healthy tissue from kidney was also used (KidB_N). Previously published in-house melanoma datasets  61   and other publicly available datasets of ovarian and prostate cancers from the 10x Visium FFPE probe hybridization based capture were used as the control in our initial phase (published elsewhere)  62  . As this approach relies on predefined gene-targeting probes, novel ncRNAs are generally not captured, although off-target lncRNA detection has been reported  62  . The coverage of the samples used in this study was an average of 100 million reads captured from about 2,000 spots, whereas for the in-house kidney and breast cancer datasets it was 100–300 million reads. Shown in detail are the results for a few cancer types (including H&N cancer, breast cancer and medulloblastoma) of the in-house spatial and public melanoma scRNA-seq datasets.     Single-cell sequencing data  Datasets from 10x Genomics, including glioblastoma, breast cancer (3’ scRNA-seq), ovarian, pancreatic, kidney cancer, melanoma and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) (5’ scRNA-seq) were used  63 – 69  .  Other previously published datasets were also used to analyze lncRNA expressions at a cell-type-specific level. These included 3′-sequencing datasets of acral and cutaneous melanoma from the study  PRJNA862451  (ref.   70  ), peripheral blood mononuclear cells from Merkel cell carcinoma (SRR7722937)  71  , patients with H&N cancer (SRR13418965, SRR13419137 and SRR13419168)  72   and 5′-sequencing datasets of tissue biopsies from patients with BCC. This included data before and after anti-PD-1 therapy from three patients (SRX5128480, SRX5128482, SRX5128486, SRX5128489, SRX5128506 and SRX5128507) out of 12 patients in the original study ( GSE123814 )  73  .    Detection of potential novel lncRNAs using an HMM-based approach  The method described by Wang et al.  10   as the TAR-scRNA-seq pipeline was adopted to identify TARs. The pipeline uses an R package GroHMM  74   that utilizes a two-state hidden Markov model (HMM) to classify regions in an aligned genome as transcriptionally active or not, based on the read coverage in each bin. The position sorted BAM files generated by the 10x SpaceRanger pipeline (SpaceRanger 1.3.0 and 2.0.1 using default parameters) were used as inputs to the pipeline (outputs from 10x Cell Ranger were used for scRNA-seq data). By default, it splits the genome into nonoverlapping bins of 50 bp and is called transcriptionally active if at least three reads were detected in that bin and were labeled as TARs. TARs found within 500 bp apart were merged into one unit. One of the limitations of this approach is that we might wrongly identify two different but adjacent transcripts as a single transcript. The regions identified were then overlapped with reference gene annotations in a strand-specific manner (reference annotations from GENCODE v.43 were used). The TARs overlapping with existing gene annotations (even a few base pairs of overlap is considered ‘annotated’ to account for extended gene boundaries) were labeled aTARs (annotated TARs) and the ones falling outside gene boundaries were called uTARs (unannotated TARs). We rule out the unannotated transcripts found on the opposite strand to that of an annotated transcript for this initial phase of the study. A count matrix of the TARs is generated with Drop-Seq tools DigitalExpression function  75  .    Analysis of sequences for coding potential, conservation and stability  To make sure that the identified transcripts were noncoding, the coding potential was analyzed using CPAT  76   and RNAsamba  20  . The FASTA sequences of the cuTARs were extracted using BEDtools  77   getfasta. CPAT was then run using the inbuilt model for the human genome. A human coding probability (HCP) cutoff of 0.364 was used as described in the tool’s documentation. HCP ≥ 0.364 indicates a coding sequence, whereas HCP < 0.364 indicates a noncoding sequence  76  . On the other hand, RNAsamba uses a neural network architecture to classify transcripts as coding or noncoding solely based on sequence information, and is robust to limitations such as truncated open reading frames, and hence more reliable.  Various metrics can help infer the functional significance of a sequence. One such metric is the conservation score, where highly evolutionarily conserved sequences tend to be associated with common essential functions across organisms, while less conserved sequences may exhibit specific functions in an organism. The conservation of the sequences were calculated using the phastCons BigWig files comprising the phastCons scores for multiple alignments of 29 primate/mammalian genome sequences to the human genome GRCh38/hg38 build ( http://hgdownload.cse.ucsc.edu/goldenPath/hg38/phastCons30way/hg38.phastCons30way.bw )  78  . The BEDtools bigWigAverageOverBed function was used extract the conservation score for each specified coordinate in a bed file.  MFE is another measure for potential functionality. In general, the lower the MFE, the more stable the secondary structure of the transcript is and hence more likely to be functional. MFE was calculated for each cuTAR in the HNC sample with RNAfold (v.2.6.4)  79   using default parameters. The most stable secondary structure is predicted.    Characterization of structure and potential functional implications  The identified uTARs were overlapped with TSS and enhancer data from FANTOM for window sizes ranging within 1.5 kb at the 5′ end. PAS data from the PolyASite database ( https://polyasite.unibas.ch/ ) curated from 3′-end scRNA-seq data was used to support the 3′ end of our cuTARs. Splice junction data from Intropolis  80   ( http://intropolis.rail.bio ), which is a database of splice junctions from analyzing 21,504 human samples sequenced on Illumina was also used to identify splice sites and hence characterize the structure of the identified cuTARs. To further validate our lncRNA identification, the cuTARs were overlapped with the new lncRNA annotations from GENCODE v.47 since release v.43, confirming that these are lncRNAs that were identified by the TAR-scRNA-seq pipeline before GENCODE annotated them as lncRNAs. Additionally, we also predict splice sites utilizing AlphaGenome  24  , a deep-learning-based tool used to predict several functional genomic features and events. It has been shown that AlphaGenome predicts splicing events with a high accuracy (Pearson correlation of up to 0.82).  The identified cuTAR reads were also overlapped with trait-associated SNPs from the GWAS catalog (all associations v.1.0.2)  81   and with GTEx CAVIAR eQTLs from the UCSC  82   table browser (downloaded on 23 August 2025)  83   with a window size of 100 kb using BEDtools to propose potential genetic-level regulation based on colocalizing features. Three sets of an equal number of random coding regions were considered and the overlap of eQTLs were calculated. There was a markedly higher overlap of cuTARs than with three sets of randomly chosen coding regions. The eQTLs overlapped with both the pan-cancer cuTARs and the cancer-specific cuTARs were identified using direct overlap (BEDtools intersect) and window sizes of 10 kb and 100 kb. The genes associated with these colocalized eQTLs were then queried in enrichR for enriched pathways, GO terms, cell-types and tissues, the significance of which were computed using Fisher’s exact test  84  .  The identified cuTARs were overlapped with active enhancers from FANTOM  85   to identify e-lncRNAs using BEDtools (500-bp window size at the 5′ end and also for the entire length of the cuTAR). These can also provide important clues about the regulatory mechanisms and potential functions of these transcripts, helping to shed light on the complex regulatory networks that govern gene expression.    Identification of cancer-specific lncRNAs  Tumor regions were identified using pathologist-provided annotations where available (for example, HNB, HNC), or inferred based on gene expression profiles when such annotations were not available (for example, CP). For analyses requiring cell-type classification (for example, BreastA), scType  86   was employed. Pathologist annotations were exported via Loupe Browser (10x Genomics) and incorporated into downstream analyses. The cuTARs differentially expressed across the annotated cancer and normal regions were identified using Seurat v.4.3 and processed using SCTransform. For FindAllMarkers function, the parameters min.pct was set to 0.1 and logfc.threshold varied between 0.1–0.25 depending on the sample analyzed. The percentage of spots in the cancerous versus healthy regions expressing the selected cuTARs were also calculated.  Few cuTARs from H&N cancer samples were shortlisted as the cuTARs of interest that could be the top potential functional candidates. They were chosen as they were (1) detected in all H&N OPSCC samples; (2) longer than 1,000 bp; (3) absent from standard annotations (GENCODE v.43) but supported by entries in other lncRNA-specific databases; and (4) differentially expressed in the cancerous region of the tissue. To be more confident about the chosen regions, we also checked their coverages in bulk RNA-seq datasets from TCGA and the scRNA-seq dataset of HNC and checked if they were detected. The bigwig RNA-seq coverage files for 96 random TCGA samples were downloaded using recount. The cuTAR coverages were extracted from these files using bigWigAverageOverBed function from UCSC Tools for the specified boundaries in a .bed file. TMM normalization was performed on the raw coverage (counts) using edgeR. By analyzing coverage, gene expression levels can be inferred. Regions with higher coverage indicate higher expression levels of the corresponding cuTARs.    Confirmation of detected signals using long-read sequencing and spatial technologies with single-cell resolution   Oxford Nanopore  Long-read sequencing with ONT was performed using the 10x Visium biotinylated 3′ cDNA libraries to validate the detection and expression patterns of the identified potential lncRNAs using PromethION flow cells. SQK-LSK110 and EXP-NBD kits from ONT were used to generate the libraries for the H&N sample C (HNC). Sequence runs were generated using super-accurate basecalling setting with MinKNOW v.22.12.5 and Guppy v.6.4.6 (flow cell type FLO-PRO002). The nanopore run generated ~16 million reads. To demultiplex the reads based on the spatial barcode, scNanoGPS  27   was used. Some changes were made to the default parameters of the pipeline with respect to the scan region, which was set to 1,000 bp as the 3′ adaptors were found that many bases away owing to longer chimeras. The lncRNAs were then identified using a modified version of the TAR-scRNA-seq pipeline, as scNanoGPS generates individual alignment files for each spatial barcode identified, rather than an individual BAM file with reads tagged with spatial/cell and UMI barcodes. Featurecounts  87   was used to generate the uTAR expression matrix. GTF annotations of the TARs from the corresponding 10x Visium dataset was also used to generate the count matrix. The identified spatial barcodes were matched with those from the 10x Visium barcode list from the tissue_positions_list.csv in the SpaceRanger output of the corresponding Visium data and only those with tissues placed on them were retained. The coordinates of the matched barcodes were also extracted from the aforementioned csv file. The expression of some potential candidates were visualized using stlearn  88   and was compared to that of the previously generated short-read data.  Further, the experiment was also performed for skin cancer samples. SQK-NBD-114.24 kit, native barcoding kit 24 V14, was used to prepare libraries for the SCC and BCC samples, which were sequenced on PromethION P24 device using R10 flow cell (FLO-PRO114M). Sequence bases were called during the sequencing run in fast-base-calling mode using PromethION software release 23.11.4 (minknow-core-promethion 5.8.3, Dorado v.7.2.13). Then, re-basecalling was performed in super-accuracy mode using Dorado (v.0.5.1). Median read length, read length N50 and median PHRED scores were computed from re-basecalled FASTQ files (Q > 10) using NanoStat (v.1.6.0)  89  . The re-basecalled reads were subsequently processed using the same downstream workflow described for HNC, including scNanoGPS analysis and cuTAR identification and visualization.     PacBio  Full-length Visium cDNA libraries were used for HiFi sequencing. Multiplexed array sequencing (MAS-Seq), a library preparation method that concatenates cDNA molecules for long-read sequencing, was used following the 10x Single Cell 3′ kit protocol (PN: 102-678-600-REV03). After cDNA amplification, cleanup and QC of 10x Visium, 225 pM cDNA per library with concentration of 23 ng μl −1  were pooled for sequencing. First, the template switching ligoonucleotide priming artifacts during cDNA synthesis were removed using biotinylated primers. Next, DNA fragments containing orientation-specific MAS segmentation adaptor sequences were generated by performing 16 parallel cDNA amplification reactions. MAS enzyme was used to create single-stranded extensions to enable directional assembly of cDNA segments into a linear array. After DNA damage repair and nuclease treatment, cDNA cleanup was performed with 1.2× SMRTbell beads.  Further, the pbcromwell workflow of SMRTlink Tools (v.12.0.0)  90   was used for to process the HiFi BAM files. With the aligned genome file from Minimap2, the TAR-scRNA-seq pipeline was run and the cuTAR expression was overlaid on the tissues and compared to that of Visium.    STOmics  Sample preparation and library construction were performed following the manufacturer’s protocol (STOmics Stereo-seq FFPE kit). In brief, stereo-seq chip slides were equilibrated to room temperature and rinsed with nuclease-free water. FFPE tissue blocks were sectioned at 5-µm thickness and mounted onto stereo-seq chip N slides (STOmics Stereo-seq OMNI). Mounted slides were baked at 42 °C for 3 h, followed by overnight incubation at 37 °C. Mounted slides were subjected to deparaffinization, H&E staining and imaging, followed by de-crosslinking to reverse formalin-induced crosslinks. Tissue sections were permeabilized to release RNA molecules, which were hybridized in situ to spatially barcoded free probes embedded on the stereo-seq chip surface, enabling unbiased capture of total RNA. On-chip reverse transcription, ligation and cDNA release were performed, after which cDNA was amplified, purified and converted into sequencing-ready libraries. Libraries were sequenced on the DNBSEQ-T7 platform (MGI Tech) and raw reads were processed using the Stereo-seq Analysis Workflow (SAW; v.8.1.3) for QC, alignment and generation of spatially resolved gene expression matrices integrated with H&E-stained images, enabling downstream analyses such as spatial clustering, cell-type annotation and visualization of coding and noncoding RNA expression at single-cell and subcellular resolution.    Takara Bio Seeker  The Takara Bio Seeker raw and processed data for human breast cancer and melanoma samples were acquired from Curio Bioscience, now part of Takara Bio USA.    RT–qPCR  Six cDNA samples from the 10x Visium libraries, including H&N samples (HNB and HNC), SCC, BCC and CRC (CP and CM) were tested for seven potential lncRNAs (cuTAR100897, cuTAR121087, cuTAR170206, cuTAR17878, cuTAR213507, cuTAR234975 and cuTAR70920).  GAPDH , a housekeeping gene and  KRT18 , an epithelial marker were used as positive controls. Two negative controls NEG1 and NEG2 were designed to target genomic regions around the centromere that do not code for RNA, hence controls for any genomic DNA contamination. H 2 O was used as a nontemplate negative control. Overall, 12 primers were designed to target seven cuTARs (Supplementary Table  4 ). The primers were designed in such a way that they did not have any off-targets using the sequence information of the HNC sample. qPCR Master Mix was prepared for each sample following the KAPA SYBR FAST qPCR kit guide to allow each well to contain 1 μl of 10 ng μl −1  cDNA, 5 μl KAPA SYBR FAST qPCR Master Mix (2×) (Roche), 0.2 μl ROX Low Reference Dye (50×) (Roche) and 3.4 μl of RNase-free water. As  GAPDH  was an endogenous control, the template for this primer was further diluted 1:8 to ensure that it was within a comparable quantifiable range. Then, 9.6 μl of the qPCR Master Mix was loaded into each well on the 96-well quantitative PCR with reverse transcription (RT–qPCR) plate before 0.4 μl of 10 nM respective lncRNA primer pairs were added. The qPCR reaction was performed with the following protocol using the ViiA7 96-well Real-Time PCR System with High Resolution Melt (Applied Biosystems); initial denaturation (98 °C for 3 min), two-step amplification (98 °C for 5 s and 63 °C for 30 s) for a total of 35 cycles with the melting curve method. The expression was calculated using the formula  C  KRT18  × CT KRT18  =  C  cuTAR  × CT cuTAR , where CT KRT18  and CT cuTAR  represent the cycle threshold (CT) values for the positive control gene KRT18 and the cuTAR target, respectively, and  C  KRT18  and  C  cuTAR  denote their corresponding normalized expression levels, calculated as described below.  The CT was normalized with that of one of the positive controls  KRT18  such that  C  KRT18  = 1. The cuTAR expression was calculated as  C  cuTAR  = 1 × CT KRT18 /CT cuTAR . The average was used for two primers targeting a same cuTAR. The expression was visualized on a heatmap (Supplementary Fig.  12 ).    Spatial autocorrelation of lncRNAs with genes relevant to cancer  SpatialDE  91   was used to identify spatially variable features. The significant spatially variable cuTARs and the top chosen candidates chosen for the H&N cancer samples were further used to measure pairwise spatial autocorrelation with coding genes using bivariate Moran’s  I  using Python scripts. Several hallmark genes relevant to cancer were retrieved from gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA)-MsigDB  92   and were used for the analysis. The spots showing (1) high expression of both the gene and the cuTAR were categorized as HH; (2) spots with gene expression and no cuTAR expression as LH; (3) ones with cuTAR expression and lack of gene expression as HL; (4) no expression of both features as LL; and (5) NS for spots with insignificant Moran’s  I . The cuTARs showing high spatial correlation (more than 50 HH spots) with genes of different hallmarks were calculated to identify the more functionally relevant cuTARs and the pathways involved.
